events.title: Assassination of Mahatma Gandhi
events.summary: On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse shoots Gandhi dead at his evening prayer in Delhi (NCERT).
events.detail:
Gandhi did not take part in the Independence Day celebrations; he was in Kolkata, working to stop the riots (NCERT). His insistence that Hindus and Muslims live in peace angered extremists. In January 1948 he undertook his last fast, partly to make the government pay Pakistan its share of assets (NCERT).

On 30 January 1948 Godse walked up to him at his evening prayer at Birla House and fired three bullets (NCERT). The government cracked down on organisations seen as responsible for communal violence (NCERT).
causes: Gandhi's fight for Hindu–Muslim unity angered extremists (NCERT).
His last fast in January 1948 (NCERT).
outcomes: The RSS was banned for a time (NCERT says the government cracked down on such organisations).
Communal tension eased; the effect was "almost magical" (NCERT).
facts: Gandhi was in Kolkata, not Delhi, on 15 August 1947 (NCERT).
30 January is observed as Martyrs' Day (Shaheed Diwas).
events.yearHook: 30 January 1948, Birla House, Delhi: 168 days after Independence.

participants.role: Announced "the light has gone out of our lives".

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"
events.before: Gandhi had fasted (January 1948) for communal peace and for Pakistan's share of cash.
events.after: **Nathuram Godse** was hanged (1949); the RSS was banned for a time. 30 January became **Martyrs' Day** (Shaheed Diwas).
events.today: His samadhi is at **Raj Ghat**, Delhi. Gandhi's titles: Mahatma (Tagore), Father of the Nation (Bose, 1944), Bapu.

events.title: Rajaji becomes Governor-General
events.summary: On 21 June 1948 C. Rajagopalachari succeeds Mountbatten as the first and last Indian Governor-General (NCERT shows Nehru's cabinet at his swearing-in).
events.detail: Mountbatten stayed on as Governor-General of the Dominion of India until June 1948. Rajaji held the post until 26 January 1950, when the office ended and Rajendra Prasad became President.
outcomes: The office of Governor-General ended on 26 January 1950.
events.yearHook: 1948 Rajaji → 1950 the post ends.

participants.role: Became President when the post of Governor-General ended.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2 "Era of One-party Dominance"
events.before: **Mountbatten** stayed on as Governor-General after 15 August 1947.
events.after: Rajaji was the only Indian Governor-General (June 1948 – January 1950); the post ended with the Republic. He later founded the **Swatantra Party** (1959) and was the first Bharat Ratna (1954, with Radhakrishnan and C. V. Raman).
events.today: Rajaji's summary of the Mahabharata and Ramayana is still widely read.

events.title: Dar Commission and JVP Committee
events.summary: The Dar Commission (1948) and then the JVP Committee — Jawaharlal, Vallabhbhai, Pattabhi (1949) — advise against linguistic states for now.
events.detail: The Congress had promised linguistic provinces since the Nagpur session of 1920. But after Partition the leaders feared that states based on language might lead to disruption (NCERT). The Linguistic Provinces Commission under S.K. Dar (report December 1948) preferred administrative convenience to language. The Congress then set up the JVP Committee of Nehru, Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya; its report (April 1949) also advised postponing the demand, but said that if the Telugu people insisted, Andhra could be formed without Madras city.
causes: Fear that linguistic states would weaken unity after Partition (NCERT).
outcomes: Opened the door to an Andhra state without Madras city.

alsoOn.text: JVP Committee report (April 1949) postpones linguistic states.

events.yearHook: Dar 1948, JVP 1949 — both said "not now".
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"; Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
facts: Order: Dhar (Dar) Commission (1948) → Visalandhra Mahasabha formed (1949) → Swami Sitaram's fast (1951) → States Reorganisation Commission (1953) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Communist leaders worked for Visalandhra even before Andhra State was formed and were a big force in Telangana politics; they supported, not opposed, linguistic states (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.before: The Congress had promised linguistic provinces since 1920, but Partition made leaders fear new divisions.
events.after: The **Dar Commission** (S. K. Dar, 1948) rejected language as the main basis. The **JVP Committee** (1949) said wait, but Andhra could be made if Madras city was given up. **Potti Sriramulu**'s fast (1952) forced the issue.
events.today: The debate is part of the APPSC Andhra-movement chronology.

events.title: Manipur merges with India
events.summary: Manipur, which held elections in June 1948 as a constitutional monarchy, is merged into India in September 1949 (NCERT).
events.detail: Maharaja Bodhachandra Singh signed the Instrument of Accession a few days before independence on the assurance of internal autonomy. Under public pressure he held elections in June 1948 — the first under universal adult franchise in India (NCERT). The Government of India persuaded him to sign a Merger Agreement in September 1949 without consulting the elected Assembly, which caused lasting resentment (NCERT).

treaties.name: Manipur Merger Agreement
terms: Manipur became part of India without consulting its elected Assembly (NCERT).

outcomes: Anger in Manipur that is still felt (NCERT).
facts: Manipur held India's first election under universal adult franchise (June 1948) (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Manipur holds elections under universal adult franchise (June 1948) (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Manipur: elections 1948, merger 1949, statehood 1972.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"
events.before: Maharaja **Bodhachandra Singh** had signed the Instrument of Accession (1947) but kept internal autonomy; Manipur held elections (1948).
events.after: The Maharaja signed the merger agreement in **Shillong** (September 1949) without consulting the elected assembly; Manipur became a Part C state, then a UT (1956) and a state (1972).
events.today: The manner of the merger is still a sore point in Manipur politics.

events.title: First general elections
events.summary: India's first general election is held from October 1951 to February 1952; the Congress wins 364 of 489 Lok Sabha seats with about 45 per cent of the votes (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Election Commission was set up in January 1950 with Sukumar Sen as the first Chief Election Commissioner (NCERT). There were about 17 crore eligible voters, most of them illiterate; parties got picture symbols and each candidate had a separate ballot box. The elections had to be postponed twice. They are called the 1952 election because most of the country voted in January 1952 (NCERT).

The Congress won 364 seats; the Communist Party came second with 16 seats (NCERT). The Bharatiya Jana Sangh (founded 1951 by Syama Prasad Mookerjee) won 3. The election became a landmark for democracy all over the world (NCERT).
causes: The Constitution gave universal adult franchise to everyone aged 21 and above.
course: 25 October 1951: polling begins in Himachal Pradesh.
Most of India votes in January 1952 (NCERT).
outcomes: Congress 364 of 489 seats with about 45% of the votes (NCERT).
Start of the "Congress system" of one-party dominance (NCERT).
facts: By 2004 India had shifted entirely to EVMs (NCERT).
Rajendra Prasad was elected President in May 1952.

alsoOn.text: Polling for the first general election begins (October 1951); the Bharatiya Jana Sangh is founded (1951) (NCERT).
Second general election: Congress again wins about three-fourths of the seats (NCERT).
Third general election: Congress keeps its dominance (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 25 October 1951 to 21 February 1952: about four months, 68 phases; 17.3 crore voters.

participants.role: First Chief Election Commissioner; ran the election (NCERT).
Lost the Bombay seat as a Scheduled Castes Federation candidate.
Got the highest votes in India (Nalgonda).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2 "Era of One-party Dominance"
events.before: The Constitution gave **universal adult franchise** (age 21 then); most voters could not read.
events.after: Parties had symbols and each had its own ballot box. The Congress won 364 of 489 seats; Nehru became the first elected PM. **Sukumar Sen** was the CEC. The **Communists** came second, strong in Telangana and Andhra.
events.today: India's elections remain the largest in the world; the voting age was cut to 18 in 1989 (61st Amendment).

events.title: Bhoodan movement begins
events.summary: Vinoba Bhave receives the first gift of land at Pochampally in Telangana on 18 April 1951, starting the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement.
events.detail: Vinoba walked through the Telangana villages hit by the armed struggle. At Pochampally (Nalgonda) the landlord Vedre Ramachandra Reddy gave 100 acres for landless Dalits. Vinoba then walked across India asking for one-sixth of every landlord's land; Gramdan (whole-village gifts) followed in 1952.
causes: Landlessness and the Telangana armed struggle.
outcomes: About 42 lakh acres pledged, though much was unfit or never distributed.
events.yearHook: 18 April 1951, Pochampalli (Nalgonda, Telangana): the first gift of 100 acres by V. Ramachandra Reddy.
events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
facts: Pre-independence rural reconstruction: Martandam (Travancore, 1921, Spencer Hatch of the YMCA) worked on "Pillars of Policy"; Gandhi's approach is reflected in Samagra Gramseva (Sevagram/Wardha); Tagore's Sriniketan (1921) and F. L. Brayne's Gurgaon experiment were others (APPSC Group-II Mains 2018 P1 key).
events.before: The **Telangana armed struggle** (1946–51) had fought over land; **Vinoba Bhave** walked through the area to find a peaceful answer.
events.after: Bhoodan (land gift) grew into **Gramdan** (village gift, 1952 onwards); about 4 million acres were pledged, but much was poor land and was never distributed.
events.today: Pochampalli is now better known for **Pochampally Ikat** sarees (GI tag) and was named a "best tourism village" by the UNWTO (2021).

events.title: SRC on Hyderabad: keep Telangana separate till 1961
events.summary: The States Reorganisation Commission's report (30 September 1955) recommends that the Telangana region remain a separate state, which could merge with Andhra after the 1961 elections if its legislature agreed by two-thirds.
events.detail: The SRC noted Telangana's fears: it was less developed in education, and its people feared being swamped in jobs by better-educated people from coastal Andhra. It also noted the advantages of a Vishalandhra. Its compromise was a separate Hyderabad State for about five years. Andhra leaders rejected the delay; the Centre chose immediate merger with safeguards.
causes: Telangana fears about jobs, education and revenue.
outcomes: Rejected; led to the Gentlemen's Agreement (1956).
events.yearHook: 1955 report said "wait till 1961"; merger came in 1956.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: Hyderabad State had joined India after **Operation Polo** (1948); its first elected CM was **Burgula Ramakrishna Rao** (1952). Andhra State wanted Telangana and Hyderabad city.
events.after: The Centre did not wait till 1961: the **Gentlemen's Agreement** (February 1956) gave safeguards, and AP was formed on 1 November 1956.
events.today: The SRC's warning about Telangana's fears was quoted again and again in 1969 and 2009–14.
events.mnemonic: SRC members "F-K-P": Fazl Ali (chair), Kunzru, Panikkar.

events.title: Gentlemen's Agreement
events.summary: On 20 February 1956 four leaders each from Andhra and Telangana sign the Gentlemen's Agreement, giving Telangana safeguards so that Andhra Pradesh can be formed.
events.detail:
The agreement was signed in Delhi. Andhra was represented by Bezawada Gopala Reddy (CM), Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, Alluri Satyanarayana Raju and Gouthu Latchanna; Telangana by Burgula Ramakrishna Rao (CM), K.V. Ranga Reddy, Marri Chenna Reddy and J.V. Narasinga Rao.

Its safeguards were later given legal backing by the Regional Committee (Article 371, 1958). Telangana leaders felt the promises were broken, which led to the 1969 agitation.
causes: The SRC's proposal to keep Telangana separate till 1961.
Telangana fears over jobs, education and revenue.

treaties.name: Gentlemen's Agreement
terms: A Regional Council (Telangana Regional Committee) for Telangana's development.
Telangana's surplus revenue to be spent in Telangana.
Domicile (Mulki) rules: 12 years' residence for Telangana jobs.
Urdu to stay in administration and courts for five years.
Education facilities in Telangana reserved for its students.
If the CM is from one region, the Deputy CM from the other; key portfolios shared.
Prohibition in Telangana as its legislators decided.

outcomes: Regional Committee set up by Presidential Order under Article 371 (1958).
Alleged breaches fed the 1969 Telangana agitation.

alsoOn.text: Telangana Regional Committee set up under Article 371 (Presidential Order, 1958).

events.yearHook: 20 February 1956 — eight months before Andhra Pradesh was born.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Cabinet posts were to be shared 60:40 between Andhra and Telangana (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.before: The SRC (1955) had suggested waiting till 1961; Telangana leaders feared losing jobs and land to better-educated Andhras.
events.after: A **Regional Committee** got legal backing under Article 371 (1958). The promise of a Telangana Deputy CM was not kept; this became a key grievance in **1969**.
events.today: Telangana leaders often cite the agreement as the first "broken promise"; it is a favourite Group-I and Group-II question.
events.mnemonic: Gentlemen's Agreement "8 men, 60:40": four from each side; cabinet 60% Andhra, 40% Telangana; a Deputy CM from the other region.

events.title: Panchsheel Agreement
events.summary: Nehru and Zhou Enlai announce the Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence, on 29 April 1954 (NCERT).
events.detail: After the Chinese revolution of 1949 India was one of the first countries to recognise the communist government (NCERT). China took control of Tibet in 1950 (NCERT). The 1954 agreement on trade with the Tibet region carried the five principles; through its clause on respecting each other's territorial integrity, India accepted China's claim over Tibet (NCERT). "Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai" was the slogan.

treaties.name: Panchsheel
terms: Mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty.
Mutual non-aggression.
Non-interference in each other's internal affairs.
Equality and mutual benefit.
Peaceful coexistence.

causes: India's wish for friendship with its giant neighbour (NCERT).
China's takeover of Tibet (1950) (NCERT).
outcomes: India conceded China's claim over Tibet (NCERT).
Friendship lasted until the border disputes of 1959–62 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: China takes control of Tibet (NCERT).
India is among the first to recognise the People's Republic of China (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 29 April 1954: the India-China agreement on Tibet trade.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: China took Tibet (1950); India gave up its old trade rights there.
events.after: "Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai" ended with the **1962 war**.
events.today: India and China marked 70 years of Panchsheel in 2024.
events.mnemonic: Panchsheel five "R-N-N-E-P": mutual Respect for territory, Non-aggression, Non-interference, Equality and mutual benefit, Peaceful co-existence.

events.title: Bandung Conference
events.summary: The Afro-Asian conference at Bandung, Indonesia (April 1955) marks the zenith of India's engagement with newly independent Asian and African nations (NCERT).
events.detail: India had convened the Asian Relations Conference in March 1947 and a conference on Indonesian freedom in 1949 (NCERT). At Bandung 29 nations met; the conference later led to the Non-Aligned Movement (NCERT). In 1956, when Britain attacked Egypt over the Suez Canal, India led the world protest (NCERT).
causes: Decolonisation in Asia and Africa (NCERT).
outcomes: Laid the base of the Non-Aligned Movement (1961) (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Suez crisis: India leads the world protest against the attack on Egypt (NCERT).

events.yearHook: April 1955, Bandung, Indonesia: 29 Asian and African countries.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: Newly free countries wanted a voice between the two blocs.
events.after: It led to **NAM** (1961). Nehru and **Zhou Enlai** both attended — the high point of India-China friendship.
events.today: The "Bandung spirit" of South-South cooperation is cited by the Global South.

events.title: Second Five Year Plan (Mahalanobis)
events.summary: The Second Plan (1956–61), drawn up by P.C. Mahalanobis, stresses heavy industry and the public sector (NCERT).
events.detail: In 1955 the Congress at Avadi declared its goal to be a "socialist pattern of society" (NCERT). The Second Plan followed: the government protected domestic industry with tariffs and built steel plants at Bhilai, Durgapur and Rourkela with Soviet, British and German help. Critics said agriculture was neglected (NCERT).
causes: Success of the First Plan.
Belief that heavy industry was the base of self-reliance (NCERT).
outcomes: Steel plants at Bhilai, Durgapur and Rourkela.
Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 reserved key industries for the state.

alsoOn.text: Avadi Congress adopts the "socialist pattern of society" (NCERT).

events.yearHook: First Plan farms (1951), Second Plan factories (1956).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 3 "Politics of Planned Development"
events.before: The First Plan had gone well; Nehru wanted fast industry.
events.after: Steel plants at **Bhilai** (Soviet), **Rourkela** (German) and **Durgapur** (British) came up; the public sector grew. Foreign exchange ran short (1957).
events.today: P. C. Mahalanobis also founded the Indian Statistical Institute; 29 June, his birthday, is Statistics Day.

events.title: First Bharat Ratna awards
events.summary: The Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, is instituted on 2 January 1954; the first awards go to C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan and C.V. Raman.
events.detail: The Padma awards were instituted at the same time. The Bharat Ratna is given on the recommendation of the Prime Minister to the President.
events.yearHook: 2 January 1954.
events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
events.before: Independent India wanted its own honours instead of British titles (Article 18 bans titles except military and academic).
events.after: The awards were paused in 1977–80; the **Balaji Raghavan** case (1995) said they are not "titles". Up to three a year; five were given in 2024.
events.today: The 2024 awards included P. V. Narasimha Rao, Charan Singh, M. S. Swaminathan, Karpoori Thakur and L. K. Advani.

events.title: First elected Communist government (Kerala)
events.summary: In March 1957 the CPI wins the Kerala Assembly election and E.M.S. Namboodiripad forms the first Communist government in India; the Centre dismisses it under Article 356 in 1959 (NCERT).
events.detail: The Communist Party won 60 of 126 seats and formed the government with the support of five independents (NCERT). Its land reforms and education bill provoked the "liberation struggle" led by the Catholic Church, the Nair Service Society and the Congress. In July 1959 the Centre dismissed the government under Article 356 (NCERT) — an early and controversial use of President's Rule.
facts: Second general election (1957): the Congress kept about three-fourths of Lok Sabha seats (NCERT).

pairs.left: First elected Communist government in India

alsoOn.text: Centre dismisses the Kerala Communist government under Article 356 (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 5 April 1957: E. M. S. Namboodiripad, one of the world's first elected Communist governments.

participants.role: Congress president (1959) who pressed for the dismissal.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2 "Era of One-party Dominance"
events.before: The States Reorganisation Act (1956) had created Kerala.
events.after: Its land reform and education bill set off the "**Liberation Struggle**" (Vimochana Samaram); the Centre dismissed it under **Article 356** (July 1959) — a classic case of misuse.
events.today: Kerala's land reforms are among the most thorough in India.

events.title: Panchayati Raj begins (Nagaur and Shadnagar)
events.summary: On the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee's advice, Nehru launches three-tier Panchayati Raj at Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959; Andhra Pradesh follows at Shadnagar on 11 October 1959.
events.detail: The Community Development Programme (1952) had failed to involve the people. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (report November 1957) recommended "democratic decentralisation" through elected village panchayats, block-level panchayat samitis and district-level zila parishads. Rajasthan was the first state, Andhra Pradesh the second. The bodies later weakened until the 73rd Amendment (1992) gave them constitutional status.
causes: Failure of the Community Development Programme (1952).
Article 40 (Directive Principle) asked states to organise village panchayats.
outcomes: Three tiers: gram panchayat, panchayat samiti, zila parishad.
Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) later proposed two tiers.
Constitutional status came with the 73rd Amendment (1992).

alsoOn.text: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommends three-tier Panchayati Raj.
Community Development Programme launched (2 October 1952).

events.yearHook: 2 October 1959 — Gandhi Jayanti; 1959 → 1992 constitutional status.

participants.role: CM of Andhra Pradesh, the second state to adopt it.

events.source: Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
events.before: The **Balwant Rai Mehta** Committee (1957) suggested three tiers.
events.after: Most states set up panchayats in the 1960s, but they faded; the **73rd Amendment** (1992) gave them constitutional status.
events.today: 2 October 1959 at Nagaur is remembered as the start of Panchayati Raj.

events.title: Dalai Lama gets asylum in India
events.summary: After an armed uprising in Tibet (1958–59) the Dalai Lama crosses into India and is granted asylum in 1959 (NCERT).
events.detail: China had annexed Tibet in 1950, removing a historical buffer between India and China (NCERT). The Chinese alleged India was allowing anti-China activity. The asylum, together with China's road through Aksai Chin, strained relations; border disputes erupted in 1960 (NCERT).
causes: Uprising in Tibet against Chinese occupation (NCERT).
outcomes: India–China relations worsened; border disputes from 1960 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Armed uprising in Tibet against Chinese occupation (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 31 March 1959: the Dalai Lama crosses into India.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: A Tibetan revolt against China failed in Lhasa (March 1959).
events.after: India gave him refuge at **Dharamshala**; relations with China soured, leading to the **1962 war**.
events.today: The Dalai Lama turned 90 in 2025; the succession question is a live India-China issue.

events.title: Indus Waters Treaty
events.summary: Nehru and Ayub Khan sign the Indus Waters Treaty at Karachi on 19 September 1960, brokered by the World Bank (NCERT).
events.detail: Partition had split the Indus river system, with the headwaters in India. After nine years of World Bank-led talks the rivers were divided: the three eastern rivers went to India and the three western rivers mostly to Pakistan. The World Bank (W.A.B. Iliff) also signed. The treaty survived the wars of 1965, 1971 and 1999.

treaties.name: Indus Waters Treaty
terms: Eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas, Sutlej — for India.
Western rivers — Indus, Jhelum, Chenab — mainly for Pakistan; India may use them for limited purposes.
A Permanent Indus Commission to meet regularly.

causes: Partition divided the Indus basin.
Dispute when India stopped canal water in 1948.
outcomes: A working arrangement despite wars (NCERT shows it as an example of cooperation).
events.yearHook: 19 September 1960, Karachi, with the World Bank's help.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: Partition split the Indus rivers between India and Pakistan.
events.after: India got the eastern rivers (**Ravi, Beas, Sutlej**), Pakistan the western ones (**Indus, Jhelum, Chenab**); India can use the western rivers for limited purposes. It survived three wars.
events.today: India put the treaty "in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack (April 2025).

events.title: Maharashtra and Gujarat formed
events.summary: After popular agitation, Bombay State is split into Maharashtra and Gujarat on 1 May 1960 (NCERT).
events.detail: The 1956 Act had kept a bilingual Bombay State. The Samyukta Maharashtra movement (with Bombay city as its demand; about 105 people died in police firing in 1956) and the Maha Gujarat movement (Indulal Yagnik) forced the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. Y.B. Chavan became the first CM of Maharashtra.
causes: The bilingual Bombay State of 1956 satisfied neither side.
outcomes: Bombay city went to Maharashtra; Gandhinagar later became Gujarat's capital.
events.yearHook: Bombay split 1960; Punjab split 1966 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"
events.before: The SRC (1955) kept Bombay as a bilingual state; the **Samyukta Maharashtra** and **Maha Gujarat** movements followed with police firing (Flora Fountain, 1956).
events.after: The **Bombay Reorganisation Act** (1960) created Maharashtra and Gujarat on 1 May 1960.
events.today: 1 May is Maharashtra Day and Gujarat Day; Hutatma Chowk (Mumbai) honours the 106 martyrs.

events.title: India–China war
events.summary: China launches a massive invasion on both disputed sectors in October 1962; India suffers a humiliating defeat, and China declares a ceasefire on 21 November (NCERT).
events.detail:
China had annexed Tibet (1950), the Dalai Lama got asylum in India (1959), and between 1957 and 1959 China built a road through Aksai Chin (NCERT). Talks between Nehru and Zhou Enlai failed. India followed a "forward policy" of posts in disputed areas.

On 20 October 1962, while the world watched the Cuban Missile Crisis, China attacked in Arunachal Pradesh (then NEFA) and in Ladakh (NCERT). Indian forces could only block the advance in the western sector; in the east the Chinese reached the entrance of the Assam plains (NCERT). China declared a unilateral ceasefire on 21 November and withdrew in the east but kept Aksai Chin. Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon resigned (NCERT).
causes: China's annexation of Tibet (1950) and the Dalai Lama's asylum (1959) (NCERT).
China's claims on Aksai Chin and NEFA; road through Aksai Chin (NCERT).
Failed talks between Nehru and Zhou Enlai.
course: Tawang and Bomdila fall in the east.
losses: About 1,400 Indian soldiers killed and nearly 4,000 captured.
outcomes: Defence spending rose; Department of Defence Production set up (November 1962) (NCERT).
The CPI split in 1964 partly over China (NCERT).
Full diplomatic relations restored only in 1976 (NCERT).
facts: Nehru wept in public when Lata Mangeshkar sang "Ai mere watan ke logo" after the war (NCERT).
The film "Haqeeqat" (1964) is set in this war (NCERT).
Vajpayee, as External Affairs Minister, visited China in 1979 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: India and China restore full diplomatic relations (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 20 October to 21 November 1962.

participants.role: President; proclaimed the first national Emergency.
His asylum (1959) was one cause of the war (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: Border disputes in **Aksai Chin** and the **McMahon Line** (NEFA); India's "forward policy"; the Dalai Lama's refuge (1959).
events.after: China declared a ceasefire and withdrew in the east but kept Aksai Chin. **Krishna Menon** resigned; defence spending rose. The **Henderson Brooks** report studied the failure.
events.today: The Line of Actual Control is still disputed (Galwan, 2020).

events.title: Kamaraj Plan
events.summary: In 1963 K. Kamaraj proposes that senior Congress leaders resign from government to rebuild the party; six chief ministers and six Union ministers step down (NCERT).
events.detail: The Congress had lost three by-elections in 1963 and was shaken by the China war. Under the plan Morarji Desai, Lal Bahadur Shastri, S.K. Patil and others quit the cabinet; Kamaraj himself resigned as Madras CM and became Congress president. The "Syndicate" of party bosses grew out of this.
outcomes: Kamaraj became Congress president and led the Syndicate (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1963 plan → 1964 Kamaraj picks Shastri.

participants.role: Resigned from the cabinet under it.
Resigned from the cabinet under it.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
events.before: After the China war (1962) the Congress was losing public trust.
events.after: Senior ministers and chief ministers (Kamaraj himself, Morarji Desai, Lal Bahadur Shastri) resigned to work for the party. After Nehru died (1964) Kamaraj, as Congress president, chose **Shastri** and later **Indira Gandhi** — the "kingmaker" role of the **Syndicate**.
events.today: Kamaraj also started the free mid-day meal in Tamil Nadu schools (1956) — a model for the national scheme.

events.title: Nagaland becomes a state
events.summary: Nagaland becomes India's 16th state on 1 December 1963 (NCERT).
events.detail: A section of the Nagas led by Angami Zapu Phizo had declared independence in 1951 and began an armed struggle (NCERT). Statehood under the 13th Amendment (Article 371A) protected Naga customary law. The north-east was further reorganised in 1972 and 1987 (NCERT).
causes: Naga demand for autonomy; armed struggle since the 1950s (NCERT).
outcomes: Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya followed in 1972; Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh in 1987 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: A section of Nagas under A.Z. Phizo declares independence (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1963 Nagaland → 1972 three more → 1987 two more (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
events.before: **A. Z. Phizo**'s Naga National Council demanded independence (1950s); the Naga Hills-Tuensang area was a part of Assam.
events.after: Nagaland became the 16th state (Article **371A** protects Naga customary law and land). The insurgency continued; the **Shillong Accord** (1975) and the NSCN-IM framework agreement (2015) followed.
events.today: The Hornbill Festival (December) is Nagaland's best-known event.

events.title: Death of Nehru; Shastri becomes PM
events.summary: Nehru dies on 27 May 1964; Gulzarilal Nanda acts as PM and Lal Bahadur Shastri, chosen through Kamaraj's consensus, becomes PM on 9 June 1964 (NCERT).
events.detail: Many feared that the succession would be messy or even that democracy would not survive, but the transfer was smooth (NCERT). Kamaraj consulted Congress leaders and MPs and found that Shastri was the consensus choice (NCERT). The same year the Communist Party split; the pro-China faction formed the CPI(M) (NCERT).
facts: CPI split in 1964; the CPI(M) was formed (NCERT).
China tested its first atom bomb in October 1964 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 27 May 1964: Nehru dies after 17 years as PM (1947–64).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
events.before: The China war (1962) had shaken Nehru; the **Kamaraj Plan** (1963) reshuffled the party.
events.after: **Gulzarilal Nanda** was acting PM twice (1964, 1966). **Lal Bahadur Shastri** became PM, led India in the **1965 war** ("Jai Jawan Jai Kisan") and died at **Tashkent** (January 1966); **Indira Gandhi** followed.
events.today: 14 November, Nehru's birthday, is Children's Day.

events.title: India–Pakistan war of 1965
events.summary: After attacks in the Rann of Kutch (April 1965) and infiltration into Kashmir (August), full war breaks out in September 1965; a UN ceasefire comes on 23 September (NCERT).
events.detail: Pakistan launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch in April 1965 (NCERT). In August it sent infiltrators into Kashmir (Operation Gibraltar), hoping for a local uprising, which did not happen (NCERT). In September Shastri ordered the army to open the Punjab front, and Indian troops reached close to Lahore (NCERT). The UN brought a ceasefire on 23 September. India inflicted considerable military loss on Pakistan, but the war added to India's economic difficulty (NCERT).
events.place: Rann of Kutch, Kashmir and Punjab
causes: Pakistan hoped to seize Kashmir after India's 1962 defeat.
Rann of Kutch clash (April 1965) (NCERT).
Operation Gibraltar infiltration (August 1965).
course: 6 September: India opens the Punjab front; troops near Lahore (NCERT).
Battle of Asal Uttar: Patton tanks destroyed.
outcomes: Department of Defence Supplies set up (November 1965) (NCERT).
facts: Shastri coined "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" (NCERT).
Anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu (January 1965) adds to the DMK's popularity (NCERT).
events.yearHook: August–September 1965.

participants.role: Gujarat CM, killed when his plane was shot down.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: Pakistan's **Operation Gibraltar** sent infiltrators into Kashmir; the **Rann of Kutch** clash came first (April 1965).
events.after: Indian forces reached near Lahore; a UN ceasefire (23 September) and the **Tashkent Agreement** (1966) followed. Shastri's "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" came from this time.
events.today: The battle of **Asal Uttar** is remembered as a big tank victory.

events.title: Tashkent Agreement
events.summary: Shastri and Ayub Khan sign the Tashkent Agreement on 10 January 1966, brokered by the Soviet Union; Shastri dies at Tashkent the next night (NCERT).
events.detail: The Soviet Premier Kosygin hosted the talks. Both sides agreed to go back to the positions before August 1965. Shastri died suddenly on 11 January 1966 (NCERT); Nanda became acting PM again, and on 24 January the Congress chose Indira Gandhi over Morarji Desai.

treaties.name: Tashkent Agreement
terms: Withdraw forces to positions held before 5 August 1965.
No use of force; settle disputes peacefully.
Restore diplomatic and economic relations; return prisoners.

causes: The 1965 war (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 10 January 1966; Shastri died at Tashkent the next night.

participants.role: Lost the leadership contest to Indira.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"; NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
events.before: The 1965 war ended in a ceasefire; the USSR offered to mediate.
events.after: Both sides went back to pre-war lines. **Gulzarilal Nanda** became acting PM, then **Indira Gandhi** (24 January 1966).
events.today: Tashkent is in Uzbekistan.

events.title: Punjab and Haryana formed
events.summary: Punjab is reorganised on 1 November 1966: a Punjabi-speaking Punjab and a new state of Haryana, with hilly areas going to Himachal Pradesh and Chandigarh a Union Territory (NCERT).
events.detail: The Akali Dal had led the movement for a Punjabi Suba since the 1950s; Master Tara Singh and Sant Fateh Singh fasted for it (NCERT). Punjab had to wait ten years longer than other states (NCERT).
causes: Punjabi Suba movement of the Akali Dal (NCERT).
outcomes: Chandigarh became a UT and the joint capital.
events.yearHook: Ten years after 1956 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
facts: The Mizo National Front begins an armed campaign for independence (1966) (NCERT).
Rupee devalued by about 57% (June 1966).
events.before: The **Punjabi Suba** movement (Master Tara Singh, Sant Fateh Singh) wanted a Punjabi-speaking state.
events.after: The **Punjab Reorganisation Act** (1966) created Punjab and Haryana; **Chandigarh** became a UT and shared capital. The river waters and Chandigarh disputes remained.
events.today: Chandigarh is still the shared capital of Punjab and Haryana.

events.title: The 1967 "political earthquake"
events.summary: In the fourth general election (February 1967) the Congress keeps a slim Lok Sabha majority with its lowest tally since 1952 and loses power in many states; observers call it a "political earthquake" (NCERT).
events.detail:
Two PMs had died in quick succession, the economy was in crisis after droughts and the 1966 devaluation, and prices were rising (NCERT). Ram Manohar Lohia's strategy of "non-Congressism" brought opposition parties together (NCERT).

The Congress won 283 Lok Sabha seats. It lost majorities in seven states and could not form governments in two more (NCERT). Coalitions of non-Congress parties — Samyukt Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments — took over in several states (NCERT). In Madras the DMK under C.N. Annadurai became the first non-Congress party to win a clear majority on its own in a state (NCERT). Defections became common; the phrase "Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram" came from Gaya Lal, a Haryana MLA who changed party three times in a fortnight (NCERT).
causes: Economic crisis: droughts, food shortage, devaluation (NCERT).
Non-Congressism (NCERT).
Weak leadership after two PMs died (NCERT).
outcomes: Era of coalitions and defections began (NCERT).
Struggle between Indira Gandhi and the Syndicate (NCERT).
facts: "Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram" — Gaya Lal of Haryana (NCERT).
Zakir Husain became President (May 1967).

alsoOn.text: Madras State is renamed Tamil Nadu (January 1969).

events.yearHook: 1967: the Congress system's first big crack (NCERT).

participants.role: Led the Congress; kept power with a reduced majority (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
events.before: Shastri's death, drought, devaluation (1966) and price rises hurt the Congress.
events.after: The Congress lost power in eight states; coalition **Samyukta Vidhayak Dal** governments came up. Defections began ("Aaya Ram Gaya Ram", Haryana, 1967). The DMK won Tamil Nadu.
events.today: Political scientist Rajni Kothari called it the end of the "Congress system".

events.title: Naxalbari uprising
events.summary: In May 1967 peasants in Naxalbari (Darjeeling district, West Bengal) rise against landlords under Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, giving the "Naxalite" movement its name.
events.detail:
A breakaway group of the CPI(M) led the uprising. In 1969 it formed the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist). The movement used guerrilla warfare against landlords; it spread to many states and was crushed with heavy force in the early 1970s (NCERT notes the Naxalite movement among the causes of tension before the Emergency).

In Andhra Pradesh the Srikakulam Girijan uprising (1967–70), led by Vempatapu Satyam and Adibhatla Kailasam, was the biggest offshoot; both leaders were killed in 1970.
causes: Landlessness and exploitation of tribal and poor peasants.
outcomes: Left-wing extremism became a lasting security problem.

alsoOn.text: CPI (Marxist-Leninist) formed by Charu Majumdar.

events.yearHook: 25 May 1967: Naxalbari (Darjeeling district, West Bengal).

participants.role: Led the uprising; founded the CPI(ML).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: Landless peasants under **Charu Majumdar** and **Kanu Sanyal** wanted land from jotedars (landlords).
events.after: The **CPI(ML)** was formed (1969). In Andhra the **Srikakulam** armed struggle (1967–70) followed; later the People's War Group (Kondapalli Seetharamaiah, 1980) and the **CPI (Maoist)** (2004).
events.today: The government aims to end Left-wing extremism by March 2026; affected districts have fallen sharply.

events.title: Telangana agitation of 1969
events.summary: In January 1969 students in Khammam start an agitation for a separate Telangana state over broken safeguards; under the Telangana Praja Samithi it becomes a mass movement in which several hundred people die.
events.detail:
Telangana people felt the Gentlemen's Agreement and the Mulki rules had been violated: jobs went to people from other regions, surplus revenue was spent elsewhere, and the Regional Committee had little power. The agitation began with student Ravindranath's fast at Khammam (January 1969) and spread to Osmania University. The Telangana Praja Samithi, soon led by Marri Chenna Reddy, took charge (May 1969). Police firing killed many; schools stayed shut for months.

Indira Gandhi announced an Eight-Point Plan (April 1969) and later a Five-Point formula. In 1971 the TPS won 10 of the 14 Telangana Lok Sabha seats, then merged with the Congress; P.V. Narasimha Rao, from Telangana, replaced Kasu Brahmananda Reddy as CM (September 1971).
causes: Violations of the Gentlemen's Agreement and Mulki rules.
Jobs and revenue grievances.
Weak Regional Committee.
course: Osmania University students join; Telangana Praja Samithi formed.
1971: TPS wins 10 of 14 Lok Sabha seats, then merges with the Congress.
losses: Several hundred killed in police firing (often given as about 370).
outcomes: Mulki rules question reached the Supreme Court (1972).

alsoOn.text: TPS wins 10 of 14 Telangana Lok Sabha seats and merges with the Congress; P.V. Narasimha Rao becomes CM (September 1971).

events.yearHook: January 1969: 13 years after AP was formed; 45 years before Telangana is created (2014).

participants.role: CM of AP during the agitation.
Became CM in 1971 as part of the settlement.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: The **Mulki rules** (jobs for locals in Hyderabad State, from the Nizam's time, 1919) and the Gentlemen's Agreement were often bypassed.
events.after: **Marri Chenna Reddy** led the **Telangana Praja Samithi**, which won 10 of 14 Telangana Lok Sabha seats in 1971, then merged with the Congress. Brahmananda Reddy was replaced by **P. V. Narasimha Rao** (1971), a Telangana man.
events.today: The Gun Park memorial (Amaraveerula Stupam) at Hyderabad remembers those killed in 1969.

events.title: Congress splits: Indira vs the Syndicate
events.summary: After Indira Gandhi backs V.V. Giri against the official candidate Neelam Sanjiva Reddy in the presidential election (August 1969), the Syndicate expels her and the Congress splits into Congress (O) and Congress (R) (NCERT).
events.detail:
The "Syndicate" was the informal group of party bosses led by K. Kamaraj, including S.K. Patil, Atulya Ghosh, S. Nijalingappa and N. Sanjiva Reddy (NCERT). When President Zakir Husain died, they nominated Speaker N. Sanjiva Reddy. Indira encouraged Vice-President V.V. Giri to stand as an independent and asked for a "conscience vote" (NCERT).

She also nationalised fourteen banks and moved to abolish the privy purses (NCERT). Morarji Desai, who had lost the Finance portfolio, left. Giri won narrowly. On 12 November 1969 Congress president Nijalingappa expelled her (NCERT). Her group was called Congress (Requisitionists), the Syndicate's Congress (Organisation) (NCERT).
causes: Rivalry between Indira Gandhi and the Syndicate (NCERT).
The 1969 presidential election (NCERT).
outcomes: Her government became a minority, relying on the Communists and DMK (NCERT).
facts: Privy purse abolition failed in the Rajya Sabha by one vote in 1970 (NCERT says it was not passed).
The 26th Amendment (1971) abolished privy purses after the 1971 victory (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Bill to abolish privy purses fails in the Rajya Sabha (NCERT).
26th Amendment abolishes the privy purses (NCERT).

events.yearHook: November 1969: three months after the presidential election (V. V. Giri won).

participants.role: Won the presidency as an independent (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
events.before: After the 1967 losses Indira Gandhi clashed with the **Syndicate** (Kamaraj, Nijalingappa, Atulya Ghosh, S. K. Patil); she backed **V. V. Giri** against the party's official candidate **N. Sanjiva Reddy** for President.
events.after: She was expelled; her **Congress (R)** kept power with Left support, nationalised 14 banks (1969), abolished privy purses (1971) and won the **1971** election ("Garibi Hatao").
events.today: N. Sanjiva Reddy of Andhra later became President unopposed (1977).

events.title: "Garibi Hatao" election of 1971
events.summary: In the mid-term election of March 1971 Indira Gandhi's Congress (R), with the slogan "Garibi Hatao", wins 352 Lok Sabha seats and routs the "Grand Alliance" (NCERT).
events.detail: Indira recommended dissolution of the Lok Sabha in December 1970 to end her dependence on other parties (NCERT). The opposition Grand Alliance of Congress (O), Samyukta Socialist Party, Jana Sangh and Swatantra had only "Indira Hatao" as its programme (NCERT). Her victory was followed by the 1971 war and sweeping state election wins in 1972 (NCERT).
causes: Congress split (1969) (NCERT).
outcomes: Restored Congress dominance, but around one leader (NCERT).
Raj Narain's petition led to the 1975 verdict (NCERT).
events.yearHook: March 1971: the first Lok Sabha election held apart from the state elections.

participants.role: Lost to her at Rae Bareli and filed an election petition (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
events.before: Indira Gandhi split the Congress (1969), nationalised banks and dissolved the Lok Sabha early.
events.after: "**Garibi Hatao**" won her 352 seats. India won the **Bangladesh war** (December 1971).
events.today: Since 1971 Lok Sabha and Assembly polls are mostly held at different times; "One Nation, One Election" bills (2024) seek to bring them together again.

events.title: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace and Friendship
events.summary: To counter the US–Pakistan–China axis, India signs a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union on 9 August 1971 (NCERT).
events.detail: Henry Kissinger, adviser to US President Nixon, had made a secret visit to China via Pakistan in July 1971 (NCERT). The treaty assured India of Soviet support if attacked. It was signed in New Delhi by External Affairs Minister Swaran Singh and Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko.

treaties.name: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace and Friendship
terms: 20 years.
Consultation if either is attacked or threatened.
No help to a third party in conflict with the other.

causes: US–China opening via Pakistan (NCERT).
Refugee crisis from East Pakistan (NCERT).
outcomes: Soviet backing in the December 1971 war.
events.yearHook: 9 August 1971: a 20-year treaty.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: The US and China were moving closer to Pakistan (Kissinger's secret trip, July 1971); refugees poured in from East Pakistan.
events.after: The treaty deterred outside powers during the **Bangladesh war**; critics said it ended non-alignment. It was replaced by a new treaty with Russia (1993).
events.today: Russia remains a major arms supplier (S-400).

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War (1971 India–Pakistan war)
events.summary: After Pakistan's crackdown in East Pakistan and an influx of about 80 lakh refugees, war breaks out on 3 December 1971; Pakistan's eastern army surrenders at Dhaka on 16 December and Bangladesh is born (NCERT).
events.detail:
In the 1970 election Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League won a majority, but the West Pakistani leaders refused to accept it (NCERT). In early 1971 the army arrested Mujib and unleashed a reign of terror (NCERT). India had to bear the burden of about 80 lakh refugees and backed the freedom struggle with moral and material support (NCERT).

Full-scale war broke out in December 1971 (NCERT). With the support of the local people, the Indian army made rapid progress and within ten days had surrounded Dhaka; about 90,000 Pakistani soldiers surrendered (NCERT). Lt Gen A.A.K. Niazi signed the surrender before Lt Gen J.S. Aurora. The US sent the Seventh Fleet into the Bay of Bengal.
events.place: East Pakistan (Bangladesh) and the western front
causes: Pakistan refused to accept the 1970 election verdict (NCERT).
Army crackdown and Mujib's arrest (NCERT).
About 80 lakh refugees in India (NCERT).
course: 3 December: Pakistani air strikes; war begins.
4 December: Indian Navy attacks Karachi (Navy Day).
facts: 16 December is Vijay Diwas.
Manekshaw became India's first Field Marshal (1973).
events.yearHook: 3–16 December 1971: 13 days; 16 December is Vijay Diwas.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: Pakistan's army cracked down in East Pakistan (March 1971); about one crore refugees came to India.
events.after: About 93,000 Pakistani soldiers surrendered at Dhaka; **Bangladesh** was born. The **Simla Agreement** (1972) followed.
events.today: Field Marshal **Sam Manekshaw** led the army; Bangladesh marks 26 March as its Independence Day.

events.title: Simla Agreement
events.summary: Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto sign the Simla (Shimla) Agreement in July 1972, formalising the return of peace (NCERT gives 3 July 1972; it was signed just after midnight of 2 July).
events.detail: The two countries agreed to settle their differences bilaterally and peacefully, and to respect the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir that resulted from the ceasefire of 17 December 1971. Forces were withdrawn from captured territory; the prisoners of war were returned under the Delhi Agreement (1973).

treaties.name: Simla Agreement
terms: Settle differences by peaceful bilateral negotiation.
Respect the Line of Control resulting from the 17 December 1971 ceasefire.
Withdraw forces to their side of the international border.
Prisoners of war returned later (Delhi Agreement, 1973).

causes: The 1971 war (NCERT).
outcomes: The ceasefire line became the Line of Control.
India insists Kashmir is a bilateral issue under this agreement.
events.yearHook: 2 July 1972, Shimla: Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
events.before: India held prisoners and Pakistani land after the 1971 war.
events.after: Both sides agreed to settle disputes **bilaterally**; the Kashmir ceasefire line became the **Line of Control**. India returned land and prisoners.
events.today: India cites Simla to reject third-party mediation on Kashmir.

events.title: Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya become states
events.summary: Under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya become states on 21 January 1972; Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh become Union Territories (NCERT).
events.detail: Meghalaya was carved out of Assam (NCERT) after the All Party Hill Leaders Conference (1960) campaign. Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became states in 1987 (NCERT). The North Eastern Council was set up in 1971.
causes: Hill tribes' demand for their own states (NCERT).
outcomes: Reorganisation of the North-East completed by 1972 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh become states (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
events.before: Assam had been split already (Nagaland 1963; Meghalaya as an autonomous state 1969).
events.after: Mizoram (after the 1986 **Mizo Accord**) and Arunachal Pradesh became states in **1987**.
events.today: The North-Eastern Council (1971) and DoNER ministry (2001) look after the region.

events.title: Six-Point Formula and Article 371-D
events.summary: To end the Telangana and Jai Andhra agitations, the Centre announces the Six-Point Formula on 21 September 1973; it is given constitutional cover by the 32nd Amendment, which adds Articles 371-D and 371-E.
events.detail: President's Rule was imposed in Andhra Pradesh on 18 January 1973 after P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned. Indira Gandhi then met leaders of both regions. The formula replaced the Mulki rules with local-area preference in education and jobs and accelerated development of backward areas. J. Vengala Rao became CM in December 1973. The 32nd Amendment (in force 1974) added Article 371-D (special provisions for AP) and 371-E (a Central University at Hyderabad). The Presidential Order of 1975 divided the state into six zones for jobs.
causes: The 1969 Telangana and 1972 Jai Andhra agitations.
The Supreme Court's Mulki rules verdict (1972).

treaties.name: Six-Point Formula
terms: Accelerated development of backward areas; state-level planning boards.
Local candidates preferred in admission to educational institutions.
Local preference in direct recruitment to non-gazetted posts (and some gazetted posts).
An administrative tribunal for service grievances.
Mulki rules and the Telangana Regional Committee to be abolished.
Constitutional amendment to give these legal force.

outcomes: President's Rule ended; J. Vengala Rao became CM (December 1973).

alsoOn.text: 32nd Amendment comes into force; University of Hyderabad established.
Presidential Order under Article 371-D divides AP into six zones.

events.yearHook: Jai Andhra 1972 → President's Rule January 1973 → formula September 1973.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: Both regions had agitated for separation (1969 and 1972–73).
events.after: The Mulki rules were replaced by **local-area preference** under the **Presidential Order** (1975), which divided AP into **six zones**. The state stayed united for 40 more years; Article 371-D still applies to both AP and Telangana.
events.today: Telangana redrew its zones (7 zones, 2018) under the same Article 371-D.
events.mnemonic: 32nd Amendment adds "D and E": 371-D (local preference in jobs and education), 371-E (a central university — University of Hyderabad, 1974).

events.title: Gujarat and Bihar movements; the railway strike
events.summary: In 1974 students' agitations in Gujarat (January) and Bihar (March), led in Bihar by Jayaprakash Narayan with the call for "Total Revolution", and a nationwide railway strike (May) challenge the Indira Gandhi government (NCERT).
events.detail:
Prices rose by 23 per cent in 1973 and 30 per cent in 1974 after the oil shock and failed monsoons (NCERT). In Gujarat students (the Nav Nirman movement) forced President's Rule, and Assembly elections were held in June 1975, which the Congress lost (NCERT). In Bihar students invited JP, who agreed on condition that the movement stay non-violent and not limited to Bihar (NCERT). He gave the call for Sampoorna Kranti (Total Revolution) and in 1975 led a people's march to Parliament (NCERT).

In May 1974 the railway employees, led by George Fernandes, struck for better pay and service conditions; the government declared it illegal and crushed it (NCERT). Congress president D.K. Barooah said "Indira is India, India is Indira" (NCERT).
causes: Price rise of 23% (1973) and 30% (1974) (NCERT).
Unemployment and corruption (NCERT).
Oil shock after the Arab–Israel war of 1973 (NCERT).
course: March 1974: Bihar students' protests; JP takes the lead (NCERT).
5 June 1974: JP's call for Total Revolution at Patna.
outcomes: Opposition united behind JP; background to the Emergency (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1974 movements → 1975 Emergency.

participants.role: Led the Bihar movement; called for Total Revolution (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"
events.before: Price rises and corruption: students in **Gujarat** (Nav Nirman, 1974) and **Bihar** rose; **George Fernandes** led a national railway strike (May 1974).
events.after: **Jayaprakash Narayan** called for "**Sampoorna Kranti**" (total revolution). The **Allahabad High Court** set aside Indira Gandhi's election (12 June 1975); the **Emergency** followed (25 June 1975).
events.today: The JP movement produced leaders like Lalu Prasad, Nitish Kumar and Sushil Modi.

events.title: Sikkim becomes India's 22nd state
events.summary: After its Assembly asks for full integration (April 1975), Sikkim becomes the 22nd state of India by the 36th Amendment on 16 May 1975 (NCERT).
events.detail: Sikkim was an Indian protectorate under the Chogyal (king). The first democratic Assembly elections (1974) were swept by the Sikkim Congress, which wanted closer integration with India (NCERT). The Assembly first sought "associate state" status (35th Amendment, 1974) and then, in April 1975, voted for full integration; a referendum endorsed it (NCERT).
causes: Democracy movement against the Chogyal (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 16 May 1975: the 36th Amendment (35th had made it an "associate state" in 1974).

participants.role: Led the integration movement; first Chief Minister (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
events.before: Sikkim was a protectorate under the Chogyal; people voted in a referendum (April 1975) to join India.
events.after: It became the 22nd state, with Article **371F** protecting its laws.
events.today: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state (2016).

events.title: Janata Party wins; first non-Congress government
events.summary: In the March 1977 election, a referendum on the Emergency, the Janata Party and its allies sweep the north; Morarji Desai becomes the first non-Congress Prime Minister (NCERT).
events.detail:
In January 1977 Indira Gandhi called elections and released opposition leaders (NCERT). Under JP's guidance the Congress (O), Bharatiya Lok Dal, Jana Sangh and Socialist Party merged into the Janata Party (NCERT). Jagjivan Ram left the Congress and formed the Congress for Democracy (NCERT).

The Congress won only 154 seats and failed to win a single seat in Bihar, UP, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi; Indira Gandhi lost Rae Bareli to Raj Narain (NCERT). The south voted differently and the Congress did well there (NCERT). Morarji Desai was chosen PM over Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram (NCERT). N. Sanjiva Reddy was elected President unopposed.
causes: Anger at Emergency excesses, especially in the north (NCERT).
Opposition unity (NCERT).
outcomes: First non-Congress government at the Centre (NCERT).
Government fell in 1979 due to infighting (NCERT).
facts: Janata Party was formed in January 1977 (NCERT).
Many states also held Assembly elections in 1977 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: March 1977: Morarji Desai becomes the first non-Congress PM, aged 81.

participants.role: Lost power and her own seat (NCERT).
Headed the inquiry into the Emergency (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"
events.before: The Emergency (1975–77) angered people; opposition parties merged into the **Janata Party**.
events.after: Indira Gandhi lost her own seat (Rae Bareli). The government passed the **44th Amendment** (1978) and appointed the **Mandal Commission** (1979).
events.today: The Janata period produced leaders of many later parties (BJP, JD, SP, RJD).

events.title: Diviseema cyclone
events.summary: A severe cyclone and tidal wave strike Diviseema in Krishna district on 19 November 1977, killing about 10,000 people.
events.detail: A storm surge about 5–6 metres high swept the low-lying Diviseema island in the Krishna delta. It was one of the worst cyclones in Andhra's history and led to better cyclone warning and shelters along the coast.
losses: About 10,000 people and lakhs of cattle killed.
outcomes: Cyclone warning systems and shelters along the coast.
events.yearHook: 19 November 1977: a storm surge strikes Diviseema (Krishna district).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: There was little warning or cyclone shelter on the Andhra coast.
events.after: About 10,000 or more people died. AP built cyclone shelters and warning systems; the response to **Hudhud** (Visakhapatnam, 2014) showed the change.
events.today: The IMD now names cyclones (since 2004 in the north Indian Ocean); evacuation saves most lives.

events.title: Janata government falls; Charan Singh PM
events.summary: The Janata Party splits; Morarji Desai resigns in July 1979 and Charan Singh becomes PM with Congress support, but resigns in August without facing the Lok Sabha, leading to fresh elections (NCERT).
events.detail: The Janata government lacked direction and leadership; rivalry among Desai, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram and the "dual membership" of former Jana Sangh members in the RSS split it (NCERT). Charan Singh was sworn in on 28 July 1979; Indira Gandhi's Congress withdrew support, and he resigned (NCERT). The Lok Sabha was dissolved.
outcomes: Mid-term election in January 1980; Indira Gandhi returned (NCERT).
Lesson: voters punish unstable, quarrelsome governments (NCERT).

pairs.left: PM who never faced the Lok Sabha

events.yearHook: 1977 Janata → 1979 split → 1980 Indira back.

participants.role: President who dissolved the Lok Sabha.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"
events.before: The Janata Party split over leadership and the "dual membership" issue (Jana Sangh members in the RSS).
events.after: **Charan Singh** became PM (July 1979) but resigned before facing Parliament — the only PM never to face the Lok Sabha. Elections followed (January 1980).
events.today: His birthday, 23 December, is Kisan Diwas (Farmers' Day); he got the Bharat Ratna in 2024.

events.title: Indira Gandhi returns; BJP is founded
events.summary: The Congress led by Indira Gandhi sweeps the January 1980 mid-term election, nearly repeating 1971 (NCERT); on 6 April 1980 former Jana Sangh members form the Bharatiya Janata Party (NCERT).
events.detail: The Janata Party suffered a comprehensive defeat, especially in the north where it had swept in 1977 (NCERT). Voters punished an unstable and quarrelsome government (NCERT). After the Janata break-up, supporters of the old Jana Sangh formed the BJP with Atal Bihari Vajpayee as president; it won only 2 seats in 1984 (NCERT). Sanjay Gandhi died in a plane crash in June 1980.
events.yearHook: 1977 out, 1980 back: 33 months in opposition.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"; NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: The Janata government collapsed (1979).
events.after: Indira Gandhi won 353 seats (January 1980). The **BJP** was founded (6 April 1980) from the former Jana Sangh, with **Vajpayee** as president. Six more banks were nationalised (April 1980).
events.today: The BJP became the largest party in the Lok Sabha in 1996 and won a majority in 2014.

events.title: Sarkaria Commission on Centre–state relations
events.summary: The Centre appoints the Sarkaria Commission in June 1983 to review Centre–state relations; its report (1988) makes 247 recommendations, including sparing use of Article 356.
events.detail: Chief Ministers such as N.T. Rama Rao of Andhra Pradesh and the Akalis demanded more powers for states. Justice R.S. Sarkaria chaired the commission, with B. Sivaraman and S.R. Sen. It recommended an Inter-State Council (set up 1990), consulting Chief Ministers on governors, and using Article 356 only as a last resort.
causes: Demands for state autonomy (Anandpur Sahib Resolution, NTR, West Bengal).
outcomes: Inter-State Council set up (1990) under Article 263.

alsoOn.text: Sarkaria Commission submits its report.

events.yearHook: Set up June 1983; report 1988.

participants.role: Led the demand for state autonomy.

events.source: Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
events.before: The **Rajamannar** report (1971) and the **Anandpur Sahib** resolution (1973) demanded more state power; Article 356 was overused.
events.after: Of its 247 suggestions, many were adopted: the **Inter-State Council** (1990), zonal councils working regularly, and caution on Article 356 (later Bommai, 1994).
events.today: It is still the main reference on Centre-state relations.

events.title: Operation Blue Star
events.summary: In June 1984 the army enters the Golden Temple in Amritsar to remove militants led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Akali Dal's Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) asked for regional autonomy (NCERT). After the Akali government was dismissed in 1980, the Akalis agitated over river waters (NCERT). Militants demanding "Khalistan" made the Golden Temple their headquarters (NCERT).

The operation (1–8 June 1984) killed the militants, but it also damaged the historic temple and deeply hurt Sikh sentiment (NCERT).
causes: Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) and Akali agitation (NCERT).
Militancy and the Khalistan demand (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Akali Dal passes the Anandpur Sahib Resolution for regional autonomy (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1–10 June 1984: army action in the Golden Temple, Amritsar.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
events.before: **Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale** and armed followers fortified the Akal Takht; the Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) and Punjab grievances had grown.
events.after: Bhindranwale was killed; the Akal Takht was damaged. Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards (31 October 1984); anti-Sikh riots followed. The **Rajiv-Longowal Accord** (1985) tried to settle Punjab.
events.today: Punjab militancy ended in the early 1990s.

events.title: Assassination of Indira Gandhi; Rajiv Gandhi PM
events.summary: Indira Gandhi is assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards on 31 October 1984 (NCERT); Rajiv Gandhi becomes PM the same day and wins 415 seats in the December 1984 election (NCERT).
events.detail:
In Delhi and other parts of north India violence broke out against the Sikh community; more than 2,000 Sikhs were killed in the capital alone (NCERT). In 2005 PM Manmohan Singh apologised in Parliament for this violence (NCERT).

Rajiv Gandhi, then 40, was sworn in by President Zail Singh. On a sympathy wave the Congress won 415 Lok Sabha seats in December 1984 (NCERT). N.T. Rama Rao's TDP became the main opposition party.
causes: Anger over Operation Blue Star (NCERT).
losses: More than 2,000 Sikhs killed in Delhi (NCERT).
outcomes: TDP the main opposition party in the Lok Sabha.
facts: 31 October is also Patel's birthday (National Unity Day).

alsoOn.text: PM Manmohan Singh apologises in Parliament for the 1984 anti-Sikh violence (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1984: Blue Star (June), assassination (October), Bhopal (December).

participants.role: His TDP became the largest opposition party (30 seats).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"; NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: Operation Blue Star (June 1984).
events.after: **Rajiv Gandhi** became PM; anti-Sikh riots killed about 3,000 in Delhi. In the December 1984 election the Congress won 404 seats (414 with later polls) — its biggest ever.
events.today: 31 October is also National Unity Day (Patel's birthday).

events.title: Bhopal gas tragedy
events.summary: On the night of 2–3 December 1984 methyl isocyanate gas leaks from the Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, killing thousands — the world's worst industrial disaster.
events.detail: About 40 tonnes of MIC escaped. Official figures put immediate deaths at about 3,800; later estimates are far higher, and lakhs were injured. Union Carbide paid $470 million in a 1989 settlement. The disaster led to the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
causes: Poor safety at the Union Carbide plant.
events.yearHook: Night of 2–3 December 1984: methyl isocyanate gas leaks from Union Carbide.
events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
events.before: Safety systems at the pesticide plant were broken or switched off.
events.after: Thousands died at once and many more later. Laws followed: **Environment (Protection) Act** (1986), and the idea of "absolute liability" (Oleum gas case, 1986).
events.today: 2 December is National Pollution Control Day.

events.title: Punjab and Assam Accords
events.summary: Rajiv Gandhi signs the Punjab Accord with Akali leader Harchand Singh Longowal (24 July 1985) and the Assam Accord with the All Assam Students' Union (15 August 1985) (NCERT).
events.detail:
Punjab: Rajiv Gandhi began a dialogue with moderate Akali leaders; the accord promised Chandigarh to Punjab, a tribunal on river waters, compensation for victims, and withdrawal of the special powers act (NCERT). Longowal was assassinated on 20 August 1985, and violence went on for nearly a decade (NCERT).

Assam: AASU had led an anti-foreigner movement since 1979, demanding that all outsiders who had come after 1951 be sent back (NCERT). The accord fixed 25 March 1971 as the cut-off date for detecting and deporting foreigners. The AASU leaders formed the Asom Gana Parishad and won power in 1985 (NCERT).

treaties.name: Punjab (Rajiv–Longowal) Accord
terms: Chandigarh to be given to Punjab.
A tribunal to settle river-water sharing.
Compensation for those killed after 1982.
Withdrawal of the Armed Forces Special Powers Act in Punjab (NCERT).

treaties.name: Assam Accord
between: AASU and the All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad
terms: Foreigners who came after 25 March 1971 to be detected and deported.
Those who came 1966–71 to lose voting rights for ten years.
Economic development of Assam.

causes: Punjab militancy (NCERT).
Assam movement against "outsiders" (1979–85) (NCERT).
outcomes: AGP came to power in Assam (1985) (NCERT).
Punjab elections in 1992 had only 24% turnout (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: AASU begins the Assam movement against foreigners (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1985: Punjab Accord in July, Assam Accord on Independence Day.

participants.role: Signed the Assam Accord; became CM (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
facts: Assam Accord signed (15 August 1985) (NCERT).
events.before: The Punjab crisis and the Assam movement (1979–85) against illegal migration from Bangladesh.
events.after: **Punjab Accord** (Rajiv-Longowal, July 1985): Longowal was killed a month later. **Assam Accord** (15 August 1985): foreigners who came after **24 March 1971** to be detected; the **AGP** won the Assam elections.
events.today: The 1971 cut-off date is behind the NRC in Assam and the Citizenship debates.

events.title: SAARC founded
events.summary: The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation is founded at Dhaka on 8 December 1985 by seven countries.
events.detail: The members were India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives; Afghanistan joined in 2007. Its secretariat is in Kathmandu. The idea came from Bangladesh's President Ziaur Rahman.
events.yearHook: 8 December 1985, Dhaka; SAARC Charter Day.
events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
events.before: Bangladesh's President **Ziaur Rahman** proposed it (1980).
events.after: Eight members (Afghanistan joined 2007); secretariat at **Kathmandu**; **SAFTA** (2006). The 2016 Islamabad summit was cancelled after Uri; no summit since 2014.
events.today: India now works more through **BIMSTEC** (1997, Bay of Bengal).

events.title: Mizo Accord; New Education Policy
events.summary: Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga sign the Mizo peace accord on 30 June 1986, ending twenty years of insurgency; Mizoram becomes a state in 1987 (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Mizo National Front, angered by the Assam government's failure during the 1959 famine in the Mizo hills, began an armed campaign for independence in 1966 (NCERT). Laldenga, who had lived in Pakistan, came back to talk. Under the accord he became Chief Minister, and Mizoram is today one of the most peaceful places in the region (NCERT).

The same year the National Policy on Education (1986) was adopted; Operation Blackboard followed in 1987.

treaties.name: Mizo Accord
terms: MNF to give up violence and surrender arms.
Statehood for Mizoram.

causes: The 1959 famine and the MNF revolt of 1966 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Revolt 1966 → accord 1986: 20 years.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
events.before: The **Mizo National Front** (Laldenga) had fought since 1966, after the Mautam famine.
events.after: The **Mizo Accord** (30 June 1986) ended 20 years of insurgency; Laldenga became CM; Mizoram became a state (1987). The **National Policy on Education** (1986) set up Navodaya schools and Operation Blackboard.
events.today: The Mizo Accord is called India's most successful peace accord.

events.title: Indo-Sri Lanka Accord and the IPKF
events.summary: Rajiv Gandhi and President J.R. Jayewardene sign the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord on 29 July 1987; the Indian Peace Keeping Force is sent to Sri Lanka and is withdrawn in 1990 after heavy losses.
events.detail: The accord tried to end the Tamil conflict by devolving power to provinces (13th Amendment of the Sri Lankan Constitution) and merging the northern and eastern provinces. The LTTE refused to disarm and fought the IPKF; about 1,200 Indian soldiers died. V.P. Singh's government withdrew the force (March 1990).

treaties.name: Indo-Sri Lanka Accord
terms: Devolution of power to provinces.
Tamil militants to surrender arms.
India to send a peacekeeping force on request.

events.yearHook: 29 July 1987: Rajiv Gandhi and J. R. Jayewardene.

participants.role: Refused to disarm; fought the IPKF.

events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
events.before: Sri Lanka's civil war with the **LTTE** sent Tamil refugees to India.
events.after: The **13th Amendment** of Sri Lanka created provincial councils; the **IPKF** fought the LTTE and left in 1990, losing about 1,200 soldiers. The LTTE later killed Rajiv Gandhi (1991).
events.today: India still presses Sri Lanka to implement the 13th Amendment.

events.title: 61st Amendment: voting age lowered to 18
events.summary: The 61st Amendment (December 1988, in force March 1989) lowers the voting age from 21 to 18 years under Article 326.
events.detail: Rajiv Gandhi's government argued that young people were literate and politically aware. About 5 crore new voters were added for the 1989 election.
outcomes: First used in the 1989 general election.
events.yearHook: 1988 (in force 1989): voting age 21 → 18.
events.source: Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
events.before: Rajiv Gandhi wanted to bring young people into politics.
events.after: About 5 crore new young voters joined for the 1989 election.
events.today: Voters can now register in advance at 17 (from 2022, four dates a year).

events.title: 1989 election: end of the "Congress system"
events.summary: The Congress is reduced from 415 to 197 seats in November 1989 (NCERT); V.P. Singh forms a National Front government on 2 December 1989 with outside support from the BJP and the Left (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Bofors scandal, the Shah Bano reversal and price rise hurt the Rajiv Gandhi government. The National Front — the Janata Dal and regional parties such as the TDP (its chairman was N.T. Rama Rao) — won 143 seats (NCERT). Both the Left and the BJP supported it to keep the Congress out (NCERT).

The elections of 1989 marked the end of what political scientists call the "Congress system", and began an era of coalitions in which no party won a clear majority until 2014 (NCERT). In Jammu and Kashmir an insurgency for a separate Kashmiri nation took hold by 1989 (NCERT).
causes: Bofors and corruption charges.
Rise of regional and OBC-based parties (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Insurgency in Jammu and Kashmir intensifies; violence by insurgents and army action through the 1990s (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 415 seats (1984) → 197 seats (1989) (NCERT).

participants.role: BJP supported the government from outside (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"; NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
events.before: The **Bofors** scandal hurt Rajiv Gandhi; V. P. Singh left the Congress.
events.after: The **National Front** (V. P. Singh) formed a government with outside support from the BJP and the Left; Mandal (1990) and the Ram temple campaign followed. NCERT calls 1989 the start of the coalition era.
events.today: No party won a Lok Sabha majority alone again until 2014.

events.title: Mandal Commission report implemented
events.summary: In August 1990 the V.P. Singh government decides to reserve 27 per cent of central government jobs for Other Backward Classes, as the Mandal Commission recommended; violent protests follow (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Janata government had appointed the Second Backward Classes Commission under B.P. Mandal (1978–79); it reported in 1980, identifying OBCs as about 52% of the population (NCERT). The report lay unused until 1990 (NCERT).

The decision led to anti-Mandal protests, including self-immolations by students (NCERT). In September 1990 L.K. Advani began a Rath Yatra from Somnath to Ayodhya; he was arrested in Bihar in October. The BJP withdrew support and V.P. Singh lost a confidence vote (7 November 1990). Chandra Shekhar became PM with Congress support. The Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation in November 1992 (NCERT).
causes: Demand for OBC reservation since the Janata years (NCERT).
The Mandal report (1980) (NCERT).
outcomes: Politics of caste and backward classes became central (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Janata government appoints the Mandal Commission (NCERT).
Mandal Commission submits its report (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 7 August 1990: V. P. Singh announces 27% OBC reservation in central jobs.

participants.role: PM whose government appointed the commission (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
