events.before: The **Mandal Commission** (B. P. Mandal, set up 1979, report 1980) found 52% of people belonged to OBCs.
events.after: Students protested (Rajiv Goswami); the Supreme Court upheld it in **Indra Sawhney** (1992) with the 50% cap and creamy layer. OBC quotas in central education came in 2006 (93rd Amendment).
events.today: OBC politics reshaped many state parties (SP, RJD, JD(U)).

events.title: Assassination of Rajiv Gandhi; P.V. Narasimha Rao PM
events.summary: Rajiv Gandhi is assassinated by an LTTE suicide bomber at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on 21 May 1991 during the election campaign (NCERT); P.V. Narasimha Rao becomes PM on 21 June 1991.
events.detail: Chandra Shekhar's government had fallen in March 1991. The Congress emerged as the largest party in the 1991 election (NCERT). P.V. Narasimha Rao of Andhra Pradesh, the first PM from South India, formed a minority government and appointed Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister.
causes: LTTE anger at the IPKF.
events.yearHook: 21 May 1991, Sriperumbudur (Tamil Nadu), by an LTTE suicide bomber.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: Rajiv's IPKF had fought the LTTE in Sri Lanka (1987–90); he was campaigning for the 1991 election.
events.after: The Congress won and **P. V. Narasimha Rao** (from Andhra, Telangana region) became PM — the first from south India — and with **Manmohan Singh** launched the **1991 reforms**.
events.today: 21 May is Anti-Terrorism Day.

events.title: Demolition at Ayodhya
events.summary: On 6 December 1992 the three-dome structure at Ayodhya is demolished; NCERT records the long dispute that ended with the Supreme Court's unanimous 5–0 verdict on 9 November 2019.
events.detail:
NCERT traces the dispute: the structure was sealed in 1949 when court proceedings began; in 1986 the Faizabad district court ordered it unlocked for worship. The BJP made the issue central to its politics, and L.K. Advani's Rath Yatra (1990) mobilised support (NCERT).

On 6 December 1992 the structure was demolished. The Centre dismissed the BJP governments of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh, and communal violence followed in many places; the Liberhan Commission was appointed to inquire. Critics saw the event as a challenge to secular democracy (NCERT). On 9 November 2019 a five-judge constitution bench of the Supreme Court gave the site for a temple and five acres elsewhere for a mosque (NCERT).
causes: Long-running title dispute (NCERT).
Mobilisation from 1986 onwards (NCERT).
outcomes: Four BJP state governments dismissed (upheld in the Bommai case, 1994).

alsoOn.text: Faizabad court orders the Ayodhya structure unlocked (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1949 sealed → 1986 unlocked → 1992 demolished → 2019 verdict (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: The Ram Janmabhoomi campaign (L. K. Advani's rath yatra, 1990) had grown.
events.after: The Babri mosque was demolished (6 December 1992); riots followed (Mumbai, 1992–93). The **Liberhan Commission** reported in 2009.
events.today: The Supreme Court's 2019 verdict gave the site for a Ram temple, consecrated in January 2024, and land elsewhere for a mosque.

events.title: National Human Rights Commission
events.summary: The National Human Rights Commission is set up on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, with Justice Ranganath Misra as its first chairperson.
events.detail: It is a statutory (not constitutional) body that inquires into violations of human rights by public servants. States set up State Human Rights Commissions.
events.yearHook: 12 October 1993, under the Protection of Human Rights Act.
events.source: Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
events.before: India faced criticism over Punjab and Kashmir; the **Paris Principles** (1991) set standards for national rights bodies.
events.after: Its chairman is a former Chief Justice (or judge, after 2019); state commissions (SHRCs) exist too (AP SHRC). It recommends — it cannot punish.
events.today: Telangana and AP each have their own SHRC after bifurcation.

events.title: Chandrababu Naidu becomes CM
events.summary: N. Chandrababu Naidu takes over the TDP and becomes Chief Minister on 1 September 1995 after most TDP MLAs desert N.T. Rama Rao.
events.detail:
NTR had returned in December 1994 with 216 of 294 seats. The rise of his wife Lakshmi Parvathi in the party angered many MLAs, who backed his son-in-law Naidu. NTR died on 18 January 1996.

Naidu promoted information technology and administrative reform: HITEC City in Hyderabad (opened 1998), the Janmabhoomi programme (1997), DWCRA women's self-help groups and the "Vision 2020" document. He was convener of the United Front (1996) and backed the NDA (1998–2004).
outcomes: Naidu ruled till 2004 and again from 2014.

alsoOn.text: N.T. Rama Rao dies (18 January 1996).
HITEC City's Cyber Towers opened in Hyderabad.

events.yearHook: 1 September 1995: Naidu takes over from his father-in-law N. T. Rama Rao after a party revolt.

participants.role: Inaugurated Cyber Towers at HITEC City (1998).

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: NTR had won the 1994 election; family and party rifts over Lakshmi Parvathi's role grew.
events.after: Naidu ran AP till 2004 with a focus on IT (**HITEC City**, 1998) and e-governance; Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy won in 2004. Naidu became CM of residual AP (2014–19) and again from 2024.
events.today: He is the longest-serving CM of (united and residual) Andhra Pradesh.

events.title: Era of coalitions: 13-day government and the United Front
events.summary: After the 1996 election the BJP is the largest party; Vajpayee's government lasts 13 days, followed by United Front governments under H.D. Deve Gowda (1996–97) and I.K. Gujral (1997–98) (NCERT).
events.detail:
No party won a majority. Vajpayee resigned before a vote of confidence (NCERT). The United Front — Janata Dal and regional parties, with Congress and Left support — took over; N. Chandrababu Naidu was its convener (NCERT). The Congress withdrew support twice.

In 1998 the BJP led a coalition government (March 1998 – April 1999), which fell by one vote; the National Democratic Alliance won in October 1999 and completed a full term (NCERT). K.R. Narayanan became the first Dalit President (1997).
causes: Decline of the Congress and rise of regional parties (NCERT).
outcomes: Regional parties became key to forming governments at the Centre (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: I.K. Gujral becomes PM (April); K.R. Narayanan becomes the first Dalit President (July 1997).
BJP-led coalition government under Vajpayee (March 1998) (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1996: three PMs in two years.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: The Congress under P. V. Narasimha Rao lost in 1996 after scandals.
events.after: Two United Front PMs followed; elections came again in 1998 and 1999. **Vajpayee**'s NDA ruled 1998–2004.
events.today: Coalition governments came back in 2024 (NDA with TDP and JD(U) support).

events.title: Kargil war
events.summary: In May–July 1999 India drives out Pakistani forces who had occupied heights on the Indian side of the Line of Control at Kargil; by 26 July 1999 India recovers most of the points (NCERT).
events.detail:
In February 1999 Vajpayee rode the bus to Lahore and signed the Lahore Declaration with Nawaz Sharif. In early 1999 several points in the Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik areas were occupied by forces claiming to be "Mujahideens"; the Indian army found that the Pakistani army was involved (NCERT).

In Operation Vijay the army and air force recaptured the peaks, including Tiger Hill (4 July). The conflict went on during May and June 1999, and by 26 July India had recovered control (NCERT). It drew international attention because both countries had tested nuclear weapons the year before (NCERT). In October 1999 General Musharraf seized power in Pakistan.
causes: Pakistani intrusion across the LoC (NCERT).
course: Operation Vijay; air strikes (Operation Safed Sagar).

treaties.name: Lahore Declaration
terms: Resolve issues including Kashmir peacefully.
Confidence-building measures on nuclear weapons.

alsoOn.text: Agra Summit between Vajpayee and Musharraf (July 2001).

events.yearHook: May–July 1999; 26 July is Kargil Vijay Diwas.

participants.role: Army chief who planned the intrusion.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
facts: NDA wins the October 1999 election; Vajpayee PM again (NCERT).
events.before: Months after the **Lahore Declaration** (February 1999), Pakistani soldiers occupied heights in Kargil.
events.after: **Operation Vijay** retook Tiger Hill and Tololing; the **Kargil Review Committee** (K. Subrahmanyam) led to the **Chief of Defence Staff** idea (created 2019).
events.today: Captain **Vikram Batra** ("Yeh dil maange more") received the Param Vir Chakra.

events.title: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand formed
events.summary: Three new states are created in November 2000: Chhattisgarh (1 November, from Madhya Pradesh), Uttarakhand (9 November, from Uttar Pradesh) and Jharkhand (15 November, from Bihar) (NCERT).
events.detail: They answered long-standing demands of tribal and hill regions for development and identity. Jharkhand was formed on Birsa Munda's birth anniversary. Uttarakhand was first named Uttaranchal (renamed 2007). Their creation without language as the basis was an argument used later in the Telangana debate.
causes: Demands of tribal and hill regions for separate states.
events.yearHook: November 2000: three states in 15 days (NCERT).

participants.role: Jharkhand was formed on his birth anniversary.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"
events.before: Tribal and hill movements had long demanded Jharkhand (Jaipal Singh), Uttarakhand (hill people) and Chhattisgarh.
events.after: India had 28 states; Telangana (2014) made 29; J&K's change to UT (2019) made it 28 again.
events.today: Jharkhand Day (15 November) is also Birsa Munda's birthday.

events.title: Telangana Rashtra Samithi founded
events.summary: K. Chandrasekhar Rao resigns as Deputy Speaker and from the TDP and founds the Telangana Rashtra Samithi on 27 April 2001 to fight for a separate Telangana.
events.detail: The TRS allied with the Congress in 2004 and joined the UPA government, with KCR as Union Labour Minister; it left in 2006 when no decision came. It became the main vehicle of the movement and won the first Telangana election in 2014 (63 of 119 seats).
events.yearHook: TRS 2001 → Telangana 2014: 13 years.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: The Telangana demand had faded after 1973; uneven growth of Hyderabad, water disputes and farmer suicides revived it in the late 1990s.
events.after: TRS joined the UPA in 2004 but left in 2006; KCR's fast (2009) brought the issue back to the top. The party was renamed **Bharat Rashtra Samithi** (BRS) in 2022.
events.today: BRS ruled Telangana 2014–2023; the Congress (Revanth Reddy) won in December 2023.

events.title: UPA government: Manmohan Singh PM
events.summary: The Congress-led United Progressive Alliance wins the 2004 election; Sonia Gandhi declines the post and Manmohan Singh becomes PM on 22 May 2004 (NCERT).
events.detail: The elections of 2004 saw a partial revival of the Congress (145 seats), which entered into coalitions in a big way (NCERT). The Left supported the UPA from outside but withdrew in July 2008 over the Indo-US nuclear deal; the government survived and completed its term (NCERT). In 2009 the Congress rose to 206 seats and the UPA returned (NCERT). In Andhra Pradesh the Congress–TRS alliance won, and Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy became CM.
facts: Left parties withdrew support in July 2008 on the Indo-US nuclear deal (NCERT).
Congress seats rose from 145 (2004) to 206 (2009) (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Left parties withdraw support over the Indo-US nuclear deal (July 2008) (NCERT).
UPA re-elected; Congress wins 206 seats (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 2004–2014: ten years of UPA.

participants.role: UPA chairperson; declined to be PM.
TRS joined the UPA; Union Labour Minister.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: The NDA's "India Shining" campaign lost; the Congress won 145 seats.
events.after: Manmohan Singh led the **UPA** (2004–14) with Left support at first; laws on **RTI** (2005), **MGNREGA** (2005), **Forest Rights** (2006), **RTE** (2009) and **Food Security** (2013). The **National Advisory Council** (Sonia Gandhi) shaped policy.
events.today: Manmohan Singh died in December 2024.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks
events.summary: Ten Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists from Pakistan attack Mumbai on 26–29 November 2008, killing 166 people; the National Investigation Agency is created in December 2008.
events.detail: They struck the CSMT railway terminus, the Taj and Oberoi hotels, Nariman House and Leopold Café. The NSG ended the siege. Ajmal Kasab, the only attacker caught alive, was hanged in 2012. Home Minister Shivraj Patil resigned; P. Chidambaram took over.
events.yearHook: 26–29 November 2008: 10 gunmen from Pakistan; 166 killed.

participants.role: Became Home Minister after the attacks.

events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
events.before: Terror attacks had hit Indian cities through the 2000s.
events.after: The **NIA** (National Investigation Agency) was set up (2008) and coastal security tightened; **Ajmal Kasab** was hanged (2012). **Tahawwur Rana** was extradited from the US (2025).
events.today: The NSG set up regional hubs (including Hyderabad) after 26/11.

events.title: Telangana movement: from KCR's fast to the Union cabinet decision
events.summary: KCR's fast from 29 November 2009 forces the Home Minister to announce on 9 December 2009 that the process of forming Telangana will begin; after the Srikrishna Committee and years of agitation, the Union cabinet approves Telangana on 3 October 2013.
events.detail:
After YSR's death (2 September 2009) the movement revived. KCR began a fast-unto-death on 29 November 2009. On 9 December P. Chidambaram announced the process; after protests in coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema, the Centre said on 23 December that wider consultation was needed.

The Srikrishna Committee (3 February 2010; report 30 December 2010) gave six options, preferring a united state with a statutory Telangana Regional Council. Agitations continued: the Million March (10 March 2011) and the Sakala Janula Samme general strike (September–October 2011). The Congress Working Committee resolved for Telangana on 30 July 2013, and the Union cabinet approved it on 3 October 2013.
causes: Old grievances over jobs, water and funds.
Political vacuum after YSR's death.
outcomes: Counter-agitation (Samaikyandhra) in coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.

alsoOn.text: Srikrishna Committee set up (3 February) and reports (30 December 2010).
Million March (10 March) and Sakala Janula Samme (September–October 2011).
CWC resolution (30 July) and Union cabinet approval (3 October 2013) for Telangana.

events.yearHook: Fast 29 November 2009 → announcement 9 December: 10 days.

participants.role: His death in September 2009 opened the way.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
events.before: **YSR**'s death in a helicopter crash (September 2009) left a political vacuum.
events.after: The **Srikrishna Committee** report (December 2010) gave six options. After the **Million March** (2011) and the **Sakala Janula Samme** (general strike, 2011), the Union cabinet approved Telangana (3 October 2013).
events.today: 9 December 2009 is remembered in Telangana as the day the promise was made.

events.title: Anti-corruption movement and the Lokpal Act
events.summary: Anna Hazare's fasts in April and August 2011 for a Jan Lokpal lead to the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (assent 1 January 2014).
events.detail: The idea of an ombudsman (Lokpal) was coined by L.M. Singhvi (1963) and recommended by the Administrative Reforms Commission under Morarji Desai (1966). Bills failed eight times from 1968. Scams such as 2G and the Commonwealth Games fuelled the 2011 movement at Jantar Mantar and Ramlila Maidan.
outcomes: First Lokpal appointed in 2019 (Justice P.C. Ghose).

alsoOn.text: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act passed (December 2013).
First Administrative Reforms Commission (Morarji Desai) recommends a Lokpal.

events.yearHook: Act passed December 2013; first Lokpal (P. C. Ghose) appointed March 2019.

participants.role: Chaired the ARC that proposed the Lokpal (1966).

events.source: Standard post-independence history (NCERT Politics Class 12; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence)
events.before: Lokpal bills had lapsed eight times since 1968; **Anna Hazare**'s fast (2011) forced action.
events.after: The Lokpal covers the PM (with limits), ministers, MPs and officials; states had to set up Lokayuktas within a year.
events.today: The Lokpal has a chairperson and up to eight members, half of them judicial.

events.title: 2014 election: BJP majority; Modi PM
events.summary: In the 16th Lok Sabha election (April–May 2014) the BJP under Narendra Modi wins 282 seats — a clear majority on its own — and Modi becomes PM on 26 May 2014 (NCERT).
events.detail:
The BJP had declared Modi, Chief Minister of Gujarat, its PM candidate in September 2013 (NCERT). It was the first single-party majority since 1984, and NCERT calls 2014 a watershed. The NDA had 336 seats; the Congress fell to 44.

In the same election the TDP–BJP alliance won residual Andhra Pradesh (Naidu CM, 8 June 2014) and the TRS won Telangana (KCR CM, 2 June 2014).
outcomes: End of the coalition era of 1989–2014 (NCERT).
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission (1 January 2015) (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1984 last single-party majority → 2014 next (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
events.before: Corruption scandals (2G, Commonwealth Games, coal) and the anti-corruption movement hurt the UPA.
events.after: Modi's government re-won in **2019** (303 BJP seats) and formed a third term in **2024** with allies (240 BJP seats).
events.today: Modi is the second PM after Nehru to win three straight terms.

events.title: Swami Sitaram's fast for Andhra State
events.summary: Swami Sitaram (Gollapudi Sitarama Sastry), a Gandhian, fasts unto death in August–September 1951 for a separate Andhra State. He gives up the fast after about five weeks on Vinoba Bhave's appeal, without any promise from the Centre.
events.detail:
Why the Andhra demand was stuck after 1947:

- The **Dar Commission** (1948) said language should not be the main basis of states.
- The **JVP Committee** (Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, 1949) said the time was not ripe, but Andhra could be formed if the Telugu people gave up their claim to **Madras city**.
- The **Partition Committee** of Madras could not agree on Madras city.

Sitaram's fast showed that people were ready to die for the cause; its failure made the next fast — **Potti Sriramulu**'s (1952) — a fight to the end.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence ch.2; P. Raghunadha Rao, History of Modern Andhra Pradesh; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1951: four years after Independence; 38 years after the first Andhra Mahasabha (1913).
events.before: The **Andhra Mahasabha** (1913) and the Congress (Nagpur 1920) had accepted language provinces; after Partition the Congress leaders feared further division.
events.after: **Potti Sriramulu** began his fast on 19 October 1952 and died on 15 December 1952; Andhra State came on 1 October 1953.
events.today: The debate between "unity first" (Dar, JVP) and "language first" (Andhra movement) is a standard Mains question on Indian federalism.
events.mnemonic: Two fasts "S-S": Sitaram (1951, gave up) and Sriramulu (1952, died). The second one won.

examAngle.point: Swami Sitaram gave up his fast-unto-death for Andhra (1951) on Vinoba Bhave's appeal.
examAngle.context: Vinoba was then walking through Telangana for **Bhoodan** (which began at Pochampalli, April 1951), so he was in the Telugu country when he appealed.

events.title: Death of Sardar Patel
events.summary: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, who brought about 560 princely states into the Indian Union, dies in Bombay on 15 December 1950.
events.detail:
In free India Patel ran the Home, States and Information ministries. He defended the **all-India services** as the "**steel frame**" of the nation, and is called the father of the civil services; 21 April (his 1947 speech to probationers) is **Civil Services Day**.

He chaired the Constituent Assembly's **Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal Areas** and the **Provincial Constitution Committee**. He warned Nehru about China in a letter (November 1950).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III ch.9; NCERT Class 12 Themes III ch.13-15; Spectrum; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 15 December 1950: 11 months after the Republic (26 January 1950).
events.before: He had integrated the princely states (1947–49), including **Hyderabad** (Operation Polo, 1948).
events.after: Nehru led alone; the **States Reorganisation** debate came after Patel's death.
events.today: The 182-metre **Statue of Unity** at Kevadia, Gujarat (2018), is the world's tallest statue; 31 October, his birthday, is **Rashtriya Ekta Diwas** (National Unity Day). He got the Bharat Ratna in 1991.
events.mnemonic: Patel's titles "S-I-U": Sardar (Bardoli women, 1928), Iron Man of India, Unifier (Statue of Unity, 2018).

events.title: Ambedkar embraces Buddhism at Nagpur and dies weeks later
events.summary: On 14 October 1956 at Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur, Ambedkar and about half a million followers take up Buddhism with 22 vows. He dies on 6 December 1956 in Delhi.
events.detail:
He had resigned as India's first Law Minister (1951) when the **Hindu Code Bill** was held up; it was later passed in parts (1955–56). He was a member of the **Rajya Sabha** (1952–56).

He got the **Bharat Ratna** after his death (1990).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence ch.1-2; Laxmikanth; Spectrum; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 14 October 1956: 2,500 years after the Buddha's parinirvana by tradition (Buddha Jayanti year); two weeks before AP is formed (1 November 1956).
events.before: He had said at **Yeola** (1935) that he would not die a Hindu.
events.after: Millions of Dalits, especially in Maharashtra, became Buddhists (Navayana). The **Republican Party of India** was formed (1957).
events.today: 6 December is **Mahaparinirvan Diwas**; the 125-foot **Statue of Social Justice** at Vijayawada (2024) is one of the tallest Ambedkar statues.

events.title: A. K. Gopalan case: the narrow reading of liberty
events.summary: In A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (May 1950) the Supreme Court holds that "procedure established by law" in Article 21 means any procedure a law lays down, and that each fundamental right stands alone.
events.detail:
Gopalan, a Communist leader, was held under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950. The court refused to read the American idea of "**due process**" into Article 21 and looked at Articles 19, 21 and 22 separately.

This was overturned 28 years later in **Maneka Gandhi** (1978), which said the procedure itself must be "fair, just and reasonable" and that Articles 14, 19 and 21 form a "golden triangle".
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1950: the first big rights case, four months after the Constitution began.
events.before: The Constitution (26 January 1950) used the Japanese phrase "procedure established by law", not the US "due process".
events.after: **Maneka Gandhi** (1978) reversed it; the **44th Amendment** (1978) made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even in an Emergency.
events.today: Article 21 now covers privacy, dignity, a clean environment, livelihood and speedy trial.
events.mnemonic: Article 21 line "G-M-P": Gopalan (1950, narrow), Maneka (1978, wide), Puttaswamy (2017, privacy).

events.title: Champakam Dorairajan case and the First Amendment
events.summary: In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (April 1951) the Supreme Court strikes down Madras's caste-based "communal G.O." for college seats and says directive principles cannot override fundamental rights.
events.detail:
The court held that DPSPs (Part IV) are not enforceable and must "conform to and run subsidiary to" the fundamental rights.

Parliament answered within two months with the **First Amendment** (1951), adding **Article 15(4)**: the state may make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: April 1951; the First Amendment followed in June 1951.
events.before: Madras had reserved college seats by community since the Justice Party's communal G.O. (1921).
events.after: The FR-DPSP balance moved step by step: **Golaknath** (1967), **25th Amendment** (Article 31C, 1971), **Kesavananda** (1973), **42nd** (1976), **Minerva Mills** (1980, harmony of the two).
events.today: Article 15(4) is the base of reservations in education for backward classes.

events.title: Shirur Mutt case: the "essential religious practices" test
events.summary: In Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Shirur Mutt (1954) the Supreme Court holds that Article 25–26 protect not only belief but practices that are essential to a religion, and that the courts decide what is essential.
events.detail:
Freedom of religion (Articles 25–28): 25 conscience and free practice; 26 manage religious affairs; 27 no tax for promoting a religion; 28 no religious instruction in fully state-funded schools.

Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24): ban on traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; no child under 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1954: four years after the Constitution.
events.before: Madras's Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (1951) put temples under state control; a math (mutt) of Udupi challenged it.
events.after: The test was used in many later cases: **Sabarimala** (2018), **triple talaq** (2017), and the **hijab** case (2022).
events.today: The essential-practices test is still debated before a larger Supreme Court bench.
events.mnemonic: Religion articles "25-26-27-28 = Practise, Manage, No tax, No teaching".

events.title: Citizenship Act, 1955
events.summary: Parliament passes the Citizenship Act (1955) under Article 11. It sets five ways to become a citizen — birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory — and three ways to lose it.
events.detail:
The Constitution itself (Articles 5–11, Part II) only said who was a citizen on 26 January 1950, including migrants from Pakistan. India has **single citizenship** (from Britain).

Loss: **renunciation**, **termination** (taking another country's citizenship), **deprivation** (by the government, e.g. for fraud).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1955: five years after the Constitution.
events.before: Part II covered only the people at the start; a law was needed for the future.
events.after: Amendments: 1986 and 2003 (stricter rules for birth), **Overseas Citizenship of India** (2003, 2005), **Citizenship Amendment Act 2019** (faster citizenship for persecuted non-Muslim minorities from three neighbours; rules 2024).
events.today: The CAA 2019 cases are before the Supreme Court.
events.mnemonic: Getting citizenship "B-D-R-N-I" (Born, Descent, Registered, Naturalised, Incorporated); losing it "R-T-D" (Renounce, Terminate, Deprive).

events.title: Official Languages Act, 1963
events.summary: The Official Languages Act (1963) lets English continue with Hindi for official Union work after 1965, when the Constitution's 15-year limit for English ran out.
events.detail:
Part XVII (Articles 343–351): Hindi in Devanagari is the official language of the Union (343); a commission and committee of Parliament (344); states choose their own (345); Supreme Court and High Court work in English unless a law says otherwise (348); Article 351 tells the Union to spread Hindi.

The **Eighth Schedule** began with 14 languages; it now has **22**. **Article 300** lets the government sue and be sued (rights and liabilities).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1963; the anti-Hindi agitations in Tamil Nadu peaked in 1965.
events.before: Tamil Nadu and other non-Hindi states feared Hindi would be forced on them after 26 January 1965.
events.after: Riots in Madras (1965) led to the 1967 amendment: English stays as long as non-Hindi states want it. The DMK won Tamil Nadu (1967).
events.today: Telugu was declared the official language of Andhra Pradesh by the AP Official Language Act (1966).

events.title: Swaran Singh Committee recommends Fundamental Duties
events.summary: During the Emergency, the Congress's Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommends adding a chapter of duties. The 42nd Amendment adds ten duties in Part IVA, Article 51A, taking the idea from the USSR.
events.detail:
The committee had proposed eight duties; the government added ten. It also suggested penalties, which were not added — the duties cannot be enforced by courts.

The ten 1976 duties include: respect the Constitution, flag and anthem; cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle; uphold sovereignty and unity; defend the country; promote harmony and renounce practices against women; preserve composite culture; protect the environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property; strive for excellence.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1976: the year of the 42nd Amendment, during the Emergency (1975–77).
events.before: The Constitution of 1950 had rights but no duties; the Emergency government wanted to stress duties.
events.after: The **86th Amendment** (2002) added the 11th duty (parents to give children aged 6–14 a chance of education). The **Verma Committee** (1999) listed laws that already enforce some duties.
events.today: 26 November (Constitution Day) is used to spread awareness of the duties.
events.mnemonic: Duties "10 in 1976 + 1 in 2002 = 11"; source: USSR.

events.title: Verma Committee on Fundamental Duties
events.summary: A committee under Justice J. S. Verma (1999) finds that many fundamental duties are already backed by laws, and suggests ways to teach them.
events.detail:
Laws it listed: the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act** (1971) for the flag and anthem; the **Protection of Civil Rights Act** (1955) against untouchability; laws against promoting enmity between groups (IPC, now BNS); the **Wildlife** (1972) and **Forest Conservation** (1980) Acts for the environment.

Courts have used the duties to read laws (for example in environment cases), though they cannot be enforced directly.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1999: 23 years after the duties were added (1976).
events.before: The duties had been in the Constitution since 1976 but were little known.
events.after: The **86th Amendment** (2002) added the 11th duty; schools added duties to civics.
events.today: The Supreme Court has said duties and rights go together (for example in the AIIMS students case, 2001).

events.title: 86th Amendment: Right to Education and the 11th duty
events.summary: The 86th Amendment (2002) makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 a fundamental right (Article 21A), changes Article 45 to early childhood care below 6, and adds the 11th fundamental duty (Article 51A(k)) for parents.
events.detail:
The right came into force with the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act**, 2009 (in force 1 April 2010). It requires private schools to keep 25% of entry seats for children from weaker sections.

The idea came from the Supreme Court's **Unnikrishnan** case (1993), which said education up to 14 is part of the right to life.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2002; the RTE Act followed in 2009 and came into force on 1 April 2010.
events.before: Article 45 had asked the state to give free education up to 14 within ten years — a target missed for 50 years.
events.after: The RTE Act (2009); the **National Education Policy 2020** extends the focus to ages 3–18.
events.today: The Samagra Shiksha scheme funds RTE in the states.
events.mnemonic: 86th Amendment "one change, three places": 21A (right), 45 (directive under 6), 51A(k) (duty).

events.title: T. M. A. Pai case on minority institutions
events.summary: An 11-judge bench in T. M. A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) holds that minorities are judged by state (not nationally) and that minority and private institutions have a right to admit students and fix fees, within reasonable rules.
events.detail:
Cultural and educational rights: **Article 29** protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens; **Article 30** gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to set up and run their own educational institutions.

Right to constitutional remedies: **Article 32** — the right to go to the Supreme Court, with five writs: **habeas corpus**, **mandamus**, **prohibition**, **certiorari**, **quo warranto**. Ambedkar called Article 32 "the heart and soul of the Constitution".
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2002: the same year as the 86th Amendment (Right to Education).
events.before: Cases from St. Xavier's (1974) onwards had left the meaning of "minority" and the limits of state control unclear.
events.after: **Inamdar** (2005) followed; the **93rd Amendment** (2005) added Article 15(5) for reservations in private institutions (not minority ones).
events.today: The Supreme Court ruled on AMU's minority status in 2024, reversing the 1967 Azeez Basha ruling.
events.mnemonic: Five writs "H-M-P-C-Q": Habeas corpus (produce the body), Mandamus (we command), Prohibition (stop), Certiorari (send the record up), Quo warranto (by what right).

events.title: First election of the President: Rajendra Prasad
events.summary: In May 1952 an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs elects Rajendra Prasad as President. He had been the provisional President since 26 January 1950, and is re-elected in 1957 — the only President to serve two terms.
events.detail:
The President (Articles 52–62) is elected indirectly by **proportional representation by single transferable vote**, secret ballot; MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry also vote (70th Amendment, 1992). Term 5 years; removed only by **impeachment** for "violation of the Constitution" (Article 61).

Powers: executive (appoints PM, governors, judges), legislative (summons Parliament, **ordinances** — Article 123), veto (absolute, suspensive, **pocket**), pardon (Article 72), emergency (352, 356, 360). He acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74, binding after the 42nd and 44th Amendments).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1952: the same year as the first Lok Sabha.
events.before: The Constituent Assembly chose a British-style president who reigns but does not rule.
events.after: Pocket veto used once by **Zail Singh** (Postal Bill, 1986). Droupadi Murmu (2022) is the first tribal President.
events.today: The 2022 election was the 16th presidential election.
events.mnemonic: Presidents who matter for exams "R-R-Z-V-N": Rajendra Prasad (2 terms), Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain (died in office, 1969), V. V. Giri (only one elected as an independent, 1969), N. Sanjiva Reddy (only one unopposed, 1977, from AP).

events.title: First Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha are formed
events.summary: After the first general elections, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is constituted on 3 April 1952 and the Lok Sabha (House of the People) on 17 April 1952; the Lok Sabha first sits on 13 May 1952 with G. V. Mavalankar as Speaker.
events.detail:
Lok Sabha: up to 550 elected members (now 543), term five years, the money-bill house; Speaker (Article 93). Rajya Sabha: up to 250 (238 elected by state MLAs + 12 nominated), a permanent house — one-third retire every two years; the Vice-President is its chairman.

Money bills (Article 110) start only in the Lok Sabha; the Speaker certifies them; the Rajya Sabha can delay them only 14 days. Qualifications: citizen, 25 years (Lok Sabha) or 30 (Rajya Sabha).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1952; the Hindi names Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha were adopted in 1954.
events.before: The Constituent Assembly itself worked as the Provisional Parliament (1950–52).
events.after: The new Parliament building was inaugurated on 28 May 2023; the old one is now Samvidhan Sadan.
events.today: The 18th Lok Sabha was elected in 2024; AP sends 25 MPs to the Lok Sabha and 11 to the Rajya Sabha.
events.mnemonic: Two houses by numbers "543-245": Lok Sabha seats now 543; Rajya Sabha now 245 (233 elected + 12 nominated).

events.title: First joint sitting of Parliament: the Dowry Prohibition Bill
events.summary: When the two houses disagree on the Dowry Prohibition Bill, the President calls the first joint sitting under Article 108 (May 1961). The Speaker presides; the bigger Lok Sabha decides.
events.detail:
Joint sittings: **1961** (Dowry Prohibition), **1978** (Banking Service Commission Repeal), **2002** (Prevention of Terrorism Act, POTA). There is **no** joint sitting for money bills or constitutional amendments.

Kinds of bills: ordinary, **money** (Article 110), **financial** (Articles 117), constitutional amendment (368).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: May 1961: the first of only three joint sittings (1961, 1978, 2002).
events.before: The Rajya Sabha could block ordinary bills; Article 108 gave a way out.
events.after: Joint sittings stay rare because ruling parties often lack a Rajya Sabha majority and avoid the test.
events.today: Article 108 cannot be used for constitutional amendments.
events.mnemonic: Joint sittings "D-B-P = 61-78-02": Dowry, Banking, POTA.

events.title: Zero Hour begins in Parliament
events.summary: In the early 1960s members begin raising urgent matters right after Question Hour, around noon — the "Zero Hour". It is an Indian innovation, not in the rules.
events.detail:
Parliament's devices: **Question Hour** (first hour: starred = oral, unstarred = written, short-notice), **Zero Hour**, **calling attention**, **adjournment motion** (Lok Sabha only, needs 50 members), **no-confidence motion** (Lok Sabha only, 50 members, no reason needed), **censure motion** (reasons needed), **cut motions** (policy cut — Re 1, economy cut, token cut of Rs 100).

Sessions: Budget, Monsoon, Winter; the gap between two sessions cannot be more than six months (Article 85).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1962: the third Lok Sabha.
events.before: Question Hour (from 1952) was the main tool to question the government.
events.after: Zero Hour is now a regular part of each day; the Rajya Sabha later moved its Question Hour to after Zero Hour (2014).
events.today: No-confidence motions were moved against the government in 2023 (defeated).
events.mnemonic: Cut motions "P-E-T": Policy (to Re 1), Economy (a fixed sum), Token (Rs 100).

events.title: Departmentally related standing committees set up; MPLADS begins
events.summary: Parliament sets up 17 departmentally related standing committees (1993) to examine the budgets and bills of ministries. The same year (December 1993) the MP Local Area Development Scheme starts.
events.detail:
Financial committees: **Public Accounts Committee** (1921; 22 members; chaired by the opposition since 1967; checks CAG reports), **Estimates Committee** (1950; 30 Lok Sabha members; "continuous economy committee"), **Committee on Public Undertakings** (1964; 22 members).

The **Union Budget** is the "Annual Financial Statement" (Article 112); money is spent only after an **Appropriation Act** (114); **vote on account** keeps money flowing for part of the year. The **railway budget** was merged with the general budget in 2017.

**MPLADS**: each MP can recommend works worth Rs 5 crore a year in his or her area; the Ministry of Statistics runs it.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1993: the year of the 73rd and 74th Amendments too.
events.before: Parliament had too little time to study every ministry's spending.
events.after: The committees grew to 24 (2004). MPLADS was paused during COVID (2020–21) to save money.
events.today: Budget day moved to 1 February (2017).
events.mnemonic: Financial committees "P-E-C = 22-30-22": PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings.

events.title: Nabam Rebia case: limits on the Governor's discretion
events.summary: In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (July 2016) a five-judge bench rules that the Arunachal Pradesh Governor wrongly advanced the Assembly session on his own; a Governor's discretion is limited to what the Constitution allows, and the Council of Ministers' advice binds him otherwise.
events.detail:
The Governor (Articles 153–167): appointed by the President, holds office "during the pleasure of the President" (Article 156); usually 5 years; must be 35. Assent to bills (Article 200): give, withhold, return, or **reserve for the President** (201). **Ordinance** power: Article 213. Discretion: reporting for President's Rule (356), reserving bills, and some Sixth Schedule matters.

The Governor has personal immunity (Article 361). The Chief Secretary heads the state civil service.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2016: the court restores the Nabam Tuki government it had overturned.
events.before: The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and Bommai (1994) had criticised partisan Governors.
events.after: In **State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor** (2025) the court set time limits for Governors to act on bills; a Presidential reference (2025) asked about this, and the court said courts cannot fix such timelines.
events.today: The Governor of Andhra Pradesh is S. Abdul Nazeer (since 2023).
events.mnemonic: Governor's bill choices "A-W-R-R": Assent, Withhold, Return, Reserve for the President.

events.title: AP Legislative Council revived
events.summary: The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council, created in 1958 and abolished in 1985 by N. T. Rama Rao's government, is revived on 30 March 2007 under Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy.
events.detail:
Article 169: Parliament creates or abolishes a Council if the state Assembly asks by a **special majority**. Council size: at most one-third of the Assembly, at least 40. Members: one-third by MLAs, one-third by local bodies, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers, the rest nominated by the Governor.

Now 6 states have Councils: AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, UP. AP's Assembly voted to abolish it in 2020, but the resolution was withdrawn in 2021.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: Created 1958 → abolished 1985 → revived 2007.
events.before: NTR saw the Council as a Congress stronghold blocking his laws.
events.after: After bifurcation (2014) AP has a 58-member Council and a 175-member Assembly.
events.today: AP's Assembly has 175 seats; Telangana's 119.
events.mnemonic: Council members by share "3-3-12-12-6" (thirds and twelfths): MLAs, local bodies, graduates, teachers, nominated.

events.title: 104th Amendment: SC/ST seats extended, Anglo-Indian nomination ended
events.summary: The 104th Amendment (December 2019, in force January 2020) extends the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and state Assemblies for ten more years, to 2030, and ends the nomination of Anglo-Indian members.
events.detail: Article 330 (Lok Sabha) and 332 (Assemblies) reserve seats for SCs and STs in proportion to population; **Article 334** sets the time limit, extended every ten years since 1960. Anglo-Indians had been nominated under Articles 331 and 333.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2019; the limit now runs to 25 January 2030.
events.before: The original Constitution reserved seats for only ten years, as the Poona Pact compromise had foreseen.
events.after: Women's seats (106th, 2023) will also be reserved within SC/ST seats.
events.today: AP Assembly: 29 SC and 7 ST seats.

events.title: The Supreme Court of India is inaugurated
events.summary: Two days after the Republic, on 28 January 1950, the Supreme Court is inaugurated in Parliament's Chamber of Princes with Chief Justice Harilal Kania and five other judges. It replaces the Federal Court (1937) and the Privy Council.
events.detail:
Articles 124–147. Jurisdiction: **original** (Centre-state disputes, Article 131), **writ** (Article 32), **appellate**, **advisory** (Article 143), and power to review its own judgments (137). Its law binds all courts (141). Judges retire at 65; removed only by Parliament for proved misbehaviour or incapacity (special majority).

India has an **integrated judiciary**: one Supreme Court, High Courts, and subordinate courts under them.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 28 January 1950; moved to its own building in 1958.
events.before: The **Federal Court** (1937, under the 1935 Act) had sat in Delhi; final appeals went to the Privy Council in London.
events.after: Its strength grew from 8 to 34 judges (2019). The **judges cases** (1981, 1993, 1998) created the collegium.
events.today: Its motto "Yato Dharmastato Jayah" (where there is dharma, there is victory).
events.mnemonic: SC jurisdiction "O-W-A-A-R": Original (131), Writ (32), Appellate, Advisory (143), Review (137).

events.title: High Court of Andhra Pradesh begins at Amaravati
events.summary: From 1 January 2019 the residual state gets its own High Court at Amaravati (Nelapadu), and the old common court at Hyderabad becomes the High Court for Telangana.
events.detail: The President's order under the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** split the common High Court. Justice C. Praveen Kumar was its first Acting Chief Justice.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1 January 2019: 4.5 years after bifurcation (2 June 2014).
events.before: AP's High Court sat at Guntur (1954–56), then at Hyderabad (1956–2018).
events.after: The three-capital plan (2020) proposed moving it to Kurnool (judicial capital); the plan was dropped (2021) and Amaravati confirmed as capital (2026 law).
events.today: A permanent High Court building is planned in the Amaravati capital region.

events.title: Legal Services Authorities Act comes into force; NALSA set up
events.summary: The Legal Services Authorities Act (1987) comes into force on 9 November 1995. It sets up NALSA (national), state and district authorities to give free legal aid and runs Lok Adalats.
events.detail:
It carries out **Article 39A** (equal justice and free legal aid), added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Free legal aid goes to women, children, SC/STs, disabled people, victims of disasters, and people with low income.

Subordinate courts (Articles 233–237): district judges are appointed by the Governor with the High Court. **Gram Nyayalayas** (2008) bring courts to villages.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 9 November 1995: now National Legal Services Day.
events.before: **Justice P. N. Bhagwati** and **V. R. Krishna Iyer** led the legal aid movement in the 1970s; **public interest litigation** began in the 1980s.
events.after: **Lok Adalat** awards are final, with no appeal. Permanent Lok Adalats for public utilities came in 2002.
events.today: National Lok Adalats settle lakhs of cases in a day.

events.title: Rajamannar Committee on state autonomy
events.summary: Tamil Nadu's DMK government sets up the Rajamannar Committee (1969) to study Centre-state relations; its report (1971) asks for more power and money for the states and the end of Article 356 misuse.
events.detail:
Seventh Schedule: **Union List** (now 98 items, originally 97), **State List** (59, originally 66), **Concurrent List** (52, originally 47). Residuary powers lie with the Union (Article 248), as in Canada.

Parliament can make laws on State List matters in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution (Article 249), during an Emergency (250), or if two or more states ask (252).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1969: two years after the 1967 elections ended Congress rule in many states.
events.before: Non-Congress governments in the states (1967) began to resent central control.
events.after: The **Anandpur Sahib Resolution** (1973) made similar demands; the Centre set up the **Sarkaria Commission** (1983).
events.today: States still demand a bigger share of taxes and less use of Governors.
events.mnemonic: Seventh Schedule "Union-State-Concurrent = 97-66-47 (1950)".

events.title: Inter-State Council set up under Article 263
events.summary: On the Sarkaria Commission's advice the President sets up the Inter-State Council (28 May 1990), chaired by the Prime Minister with all Chief Ministers, to discuss Centre-state issues.
events.detail: Administrative relations: Articles 256–263 — states must obey Union laws (256); the Union can give directions (257); **all-India services** (312). Coordination bodies: **zonal councils** (1956, States Reorganisation Act), the **NITI Aayog** Governing Council, **GST Council**. Water disputes: **Article 262** and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act (1956).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1990: seven years after the Sarkaria Commission was set up.
events.before: Sarkaria (report 1988) had asked for a permanent forum.
events.after: The Council meets rarely (the 11th meeting was in 2016).
events.today: AP is in the Southern Zonal Council with Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry.

events.title: 69th Amendment: special status for Delhi
events.summary: The 69th Amendment (1991) adds Article 239AA, making Delhi the National Capital Territory with its own elected Assembly and Council of Ministers, but with police, public order and land under the Centre.
events.detail:
Union Territories (Part VIII, Articles 239–241) are run by the President through an administrator. Delhi, Puducherry and (since 2019) Jammu and Kashmir have legislatures.

**Fifth Schedule**: Scheduled Areas and tribes in most states (Tribes Advisory Councils). **Sixth Schedule**: autonomous district councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1991: Delhi's first Assembly election followed in 1993.
events.before: Delhi had a Metropolitan Council (1966) with few powers; the Balakrishnan Committee (1989) suggested an assembly.
events.after: The Supreme Court (2018, 2023) said the elected government controls services; Parliament then passed the GNCTD Amendment Act (2023) giving the Centre more say.
events.today: India has 8 Union Territories.
events.mnemonic: UTs with assemblies "D-P-J": Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir.

events.title: Punchhi Commission on Centre-state relations
events.summary: The second commission on Centre-state relations, under Justice M. M. Punchhi, is set up in 2007 and reports in 2010.
events.detail:
It suggested fixed five-year terms for Governors, removal only by a resolution of the state Assembly, and "localised emergency" provisions so that a whole state need not be put under President's Rule.

Financial relations: taxes shared through the **Finance Commission** (Article 280); grants under Articles 275 and 282; GST shared under Article 269A and 270.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2007; report March 2010.
events.before: The **Sarkaria Commission** (1983–88) was the first; the **Rajamannar** (1969) was a state-level one.
events.after: Many of its ideas are still under discussion; none on Governors has been adopted.
events.today: The 16th Finance Commission (Arvind Panagariya) reported for 2026–31.

events.title: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommends three-tier Panchayati Raj
events.summary: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (report November 1957), studying why the Community Development Programme failed, recommends "democratic decentralisation": elected village panchayats, block panchayat samitis and district zila parishads.
events.detail: Committees on local government: **Balwant Rai Mehta** (1957, three tiers), **Ashok Mehta** (1977, two tiers, parties may contest), **G. V. K. Rao** (1985, district as the key unit), **L. M. Singhvi** (1986, constitutional status), **Thungon** (1988, constitutional status).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1957: Rajasthan starts Panchayati Raj two years later (1959).
events.before: Gandhi wanted **gram swaraj**; Article 40 (DPSP) asked states to organise village panchayats; the **Community Development Programme** (1952) failed to involve people.
events.after: Nagaur (Rajasthan) and Shadnagar (AP) began Panchayati Raj in October 1959.
events.today: 24 April is National Panchayati Raj Day (the day the 73rd Amendment came into force).
events.mnemonic: PR committees "B-A-G-L-T": Balwant Rai (57), Ashok (77), GVK Rao (85), L M Singhvi (86), Thungon (88).

events.title: Ashok Mehta Committee on Panchayati Raj
events.summary: The Janata government's Ashok Mehta Committee (December 1977, report 1978) suggests two tiers — mandal panchayats and zila parishads — official party participation, and constitutional recognition.
events.detail: Its mandal idea was taken up by Karnataka, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh. Local self-government's roots: **Chola village assemblies** (Uttaramerur, about 920), **Ripon**'s Resolution (1882), the **Royal Commission on Decentralisation** (1907).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1977: 20 years after Balwant Rai Mehta.
events.before: Panchayats had weakened in the 1960s–70s; elections were not held regularly.
events.after: AP formed **mandals** in place of taluks (1985) and mandal praja parishads (1986).
events.today: West Bengal (1978) was the first state to hold party-based panchayat elections.

events.title: NTR replaces taluks with mandals in Andhra Pradesh
events.summary: In 1985 N. T. Rama Rao's government replaces about 300 taluks and samitis with over 1,100 smaller mandals, bringing government offices closer to villages. Mandal Praja Parishads follow in 1986.
events.detail: AP local government in order: Panchayati Raj from **Shadnagar** (1959); **mandals** (1985); the **AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994** (after the 73rd Amendment): gram panchayat, mandal parishad and zilla parishad; **village and ward secretariats** (2019).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 25 May 1985: two years after NTR came to power (1983).
events.before: The **Ashok Mehta** Committee (1978) had suggested mandal panchayats.
events.after: The 1994 Act followed the 73rd Amendment. The **Mandal Revenue Officer** (now tahsildar) runs revenue at mandal level.
events.today: AP has about 680 mandals across 28 districts.

events.title: 74th Amendment: municipalities get constitutional status
events.summary: The 74th Amendment comes into force on 1 June 1993, adding Part IXA (Articles 243P–243ZG) and the Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects) for municipalities.
events.detail: Three types: **nagar panchayat** (area moving from rural to urban), **municipal council** (smaller town), **municipal corporation** (big city). Also: **ward committees**, **District Planning Committee** (243ZD), **Metropolitan Planning Committee** (243ZE), State Election Commission and State Finance Commission (shared with Part IX).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1 June 1993: five weeks after the 73rd Amendment came into force (24 April 1993).
events.before: Municipalities had existed since **Madras** (1687), the oldest corporation, but states could supersede them at will.
events.after: Missions like **JNNURM** (2005), **Smart Cities** and **AMRUT** (2015) funded cities.
events.today: Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation is AP's largest.
events.mnemonic: Urban bodies by size "N-C-C": Nagar panchayat, municipal Council, municipal Corporation.

events.title: PESA Act: panchayats for Scheduled Areas
events.summary: The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act (24 December 1996), based on the Bhuria Committee, extends Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with special powers for the gram sabha over land, forests, minor minerals and money-lending.
events.detail:
The gram sabha must be consulted before land is acquired in Scheduled Areas; it owns minor forest produce and can stop the sale of liquor. PESA covers 10 states, including **Andhra Pradesh** and **Telangana** (AP framed its PESA rules in 2011).

Related: the **Forest Rights Act** (2006) gives forest dwellers rights over land and forest produce.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 24 December 1996: three years after the 73rd Amendment.
events.before: The 73rd Amendment (Article 243M) left Scheduled Areas out until Parliament made a special law.
events.after: The **Samatha** judgment (1997, AP) held that tribal land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to private miners.
events.today: The Agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam districts are under PESA.

events.title: AP village and ward secretariats begin
events.summary: On 2 October 2019 Andhra Pradesh starts village and ward secretariats — about 15,000 offices, each serving about 2,000 people, with about ten staff and a network of volunteers delivering welfare at the doorstep.
events.detail: They work under the gram panchayats and municipalities and deliver over 500 services. AP's local bodies: about 13,000 gram panchayats, 660 mandal parishads, 13 zilla parishads (the old districts), and urban local bodies.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2 October 2019: Gandhi Jayanti, 150th year.
events.before: Panchayats had few staff; welfare reached people through mandal offices.
events.after: The system continues under new names and rules after 2024.
events.today: The model is studied by other states as "doorstep governance".

events.title: 65th Amendment: a National Commission for SCs and STs
events.summary: The 65th Amendment (1990) replaces the single Special Officer for SCs and STs with a multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs (Article 338). The 89th Amendment (2003) splits it into the NCSC (338) and NCST (338A, from 2004).
events.detail: Other law officers: the **Attorney General** (Article 76, the government's chief lawyer, can speak in Parliament but not vote), the **Advocate General** of a state (165), the **Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities** (350B).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1990: the same year the Mandal report was implemented.
events.before: A Special Commissioner (1950) reported on SC/ST safeguards.
events.after: The **NCBC** got constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018).
events.today: The commissions have the powers of a civil court when they inquire into complaints.
events.mnemonic: Commissions by article "338-338A-338B": SCs, STs, Backward Classes.

events.title: Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners Act, 2023
events.summary: After the Supreme Court (Anoop Baranwal, March 2023) asked for a neutral process, Parliament passes a law (December 2023): the CEC and Election Commissioners are chosen by a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and a Union minister.
events.detail:
The Election Commission (Article 324) was a one-member body until 1989; it became multi-member (CEC + 2 ECs) in 1989 briefly and permanently from 1993. The CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge.

Reforms: **EVMs** (first used 1982 at Paravur, Kerala; all-India 2004), **VVPAT** (2013), **NOTA** (2013), **Model Code of Conduct** (from 1960, Kerala).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2023; the first appointments under the law were made in March 2024.
events.before: The government alone chose election commissioners.
events.after: Petitions challenging the new law are before the Supreme Court.
events.today: The Election Commission ran the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls (2025).

events.title: Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission formed
events.summary: With the new state on 1 November 1956, the Andhra Public Service Commission (1953, Kurnool) and the Hyderabad PSC are merged into the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission under Article 315.
events.detail:
State PSCs (Articles 315–323): the chairman and members are appointed by the **Governor** but can be removed only by the **President** (after a Supreme Court inquiry for misbehaviour). They retire at 62 (UPSC members at 65). Article 320 lists their duties: exams, advice on recruitment, promotions and discipline.

After 2014 residual AP kept APPSC (Vijayawada) and Telangana formed **TSPSC** (now TGPSC).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D. D. Basu; NCERT Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1 November 1956: the day AP was formed.
events.before: The **Public Service Commission** idea began with the Lee Commission (1924) and the 1935 Act.
events.after: APPSC holds Group-I, Group-II and other exams for state services.
events.today: APPSC's office is at Vijayawada.

events.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.summary: The UN General Assembly adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948 — 30 articles of rights for every person. India's Hansa Mehta gets "all men" changed to "all human beings".
events.detail:
The UDHR is not a treaty, but two covenants (1966) made it binding: **ICCPR** (civil and political) and **ICESCR** (economic, social, cultural). Others India has joined: **CEDAW** (women, 1993), **CRC** (children, 1992), **CRPD** (disability, 2007). India signed but has not ratified the **Convention against Torture** (1997).

The **UN Human Rights Council** (2006, Geneva) replaced the Human Rights Commission.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 10 December 1948: now Human Rights Day.
events.before: The horrors of World War II; the UN Charter (1945) promised to protect human rights. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting.
events.after: India's Fundamental Rights (1950) match many UDHR articles. The **Protection of Human Rights Act** (1993) set up the NHRC.
events.today: The UDHR is the most translated document in the world.
events.mnemonic: UN rights treaties India joined "C-C-C": CEDAW (women), CRC (children), CRPD (disability).

events.title: Consumer Protection Act, 1986
events.summary: The Consumer Protection Act (24 December 1986) gives buyers six rights and sets up cheap, quick consumer courts at district, state and national levels.
events.detail:
Six rights: safety, information, choice, to be heard, redressal, consumer education. The **2019 Act** replaced it: a **Central Consumer Protection Authority**, e-commerce rules, product liability, and filing complaints online. Limits (2021): district up to Rs 50 lakh, state up to Rs 2 crore, national above.

Right to education: Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) and the RTE Act (2009).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 24 December 1986: now National Consumer Day (15 March is World Consumer Rights Day).
events.before: Consumers had to go to slow civil courts.
events.after: The 2019 Act brought e-commerce and misleading ads under control.
events.today: The e-Daakhil portal lets people file consumer cases online.

events.title: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
events.summary: Parliament passes the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989), with special courts and stricter punishment for crimes against SCs and STs.
events.detail:
Older law: the **Untouchability (Offences) Act** (1955), renamed the **Protection of Civil Rights Act** (1976), under **Article 17**. In **Subhash Kashinath Mahajan** (2018) the court diluted the arrest rules; Parliament restored them (2018 amendment, upheld in 2020).

Other groups: the **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act** (2016, 21 disabilities, 4% job quota), the **Transgender Persons Act** (2019), the **Senior Citizens Act** (2007).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1989: 34 years after the 1955 Untouchability law.
events.before: The **Karamchedu** massacre (1985, Prakasam district, AP) and similar crimes showed the old law was weak.
events.after: The **Tsundur** case (1991, Guntur) was tried under the new law. Rules were strengthened in 2015–16.
events.today: Special courts and exclusive public prosecutors are required in each district with many cases.

events.title: POCSO Act protects children from sexual offences
events.summary: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (2012) makes child-friendly rules for reporting, recording evidence and trial, for victims under 18.
events.detail:
Child rights: Articles 15(3), 21A, 24, 39(e)–(f), 45. Laws: **Juvenile Justice Act** (2015; 16–18-year-olds can be tried as adults for heinous crimes), **Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act** (2016; no child under 14 in any work, no 14–18 in hazardous work), **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act** (2006).

Women: **Dowry Prohibition** (1961), **Domestic Violence Act** (2005), **POSH** (2013), the 2013 criminal law amendment after the Delhi case (2012); the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (2024) has a separate chapter on crimes against women and children.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2012; amended in 2019 to add the death penalty for aggravated cases.
events.before: Child abuse was dealt with under the general IPC, which did not cover many crimes against boys.
events.after: The **National Commission for Protection of Child Rights** (2007) monitors it; fast-track POCSO courts were set up (2019).
events.today: Telangana runs "Bharosa" centres for women and child victims.

events.title: The Central Bureau of Investigation is set up
events.summary: On 1 April 1963 a government resolution sets up the CBI, growing out of the Special Police Establishment (1941). It draws its legal power from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.
events.detail:
The CBI is not a statutory body; it needs the state's consent to work in a state (several states have withdrawn general consent). Its director is chosen by a committee of the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and the CJI (Lokpal Act, 2013), for two years at least (Vineet Narain, 1997).

Anti-corruption chain: **CBI** (1963) → **CVC** (1964; statutory 2003) → **Lokpal** (2013, working 2019) and state **Lokayuktas** (first: Maharashtra, 1971).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1 April 1963: one year after the Santhanam Committee began.
events.before: The Special Police Establishment (1941) checked bribery in war supplies.
events.after: The **Vineet Narain** case (1997, "Jain hawala") gave the CBI and CVC more independence; the court once called the CBI a "caged parrot" (2013).
events.today: India's police link to Interpol runs through the CBI.
events.mnemonic: Watchdogs by year "S-C-C-L": SPE (1941), CBI (1963), CVC (1964), Lokpal (2013).

events.title: Central Vigilance Commission set up on the Santhanam Committee's advice
events.summary: The Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1962–64) leads to the Central Vigilance Commission (February 1964). It became statutory under the CVC Act, 2003.
events.detail:
Body types: **constitutional** (in the Constitution: ECI, UPSC, CAG, FC), **statutory** (made by an Act: NHRC, CVC, CIC, NGT, SEBI), **executive** (by government order: NITI Aayog, once the CBI and Planning Commission).

Others: **CIC** (RTI Act 2005), **Law Commission** (first after 1947 in 1955, under M. C. Setalvad; an executive body).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1964: the CVC was a recommendation of the Santhanam Committee.
events.before: Corruption cases in the 1950s (jeep scandal, Mundhra deal) worried Parliament.
events.after: The CVC got statutory power (2003) and oversight of the CBI's anti-corruption work; it also hears **whistleblower** complaints (2004 resolution).
events.today: Vigilance Awareness Week is held around Patel's birthday (31 October).
events.mnemonic: Body types "C-S-E": Constitutional (in the Constitution), Statutory (by an Act), Executive (by an order).

events.title: National Green Tribunal set up
events.summary: The National Green Tribunal Act (2010) sets up a special court for environment cases (18 October 2010), with judges and experts, which must decide cases within six months.
events.detail:
Tribunals: **Article 323A** (administrative — the **Central Administrative Tribunal**, 1985) and **323B** (tax, land, elections and others), both added by the 42nd Amendment. The **Tribunals Reforms Act** (2021) merged several tribunals.

Regulators: **SEBI** (1992), **TRAI** (1997), **IRDAI** (1999), **CCI** (2002/2009), **PFRDA** (2013), **RBI** (1935).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2010: India became the third country with a green tribunal, after Australia and New Zealand.
events.before: The Supreme Court had suggested environment courts (M. C. Mehta cases, 1986).
events.after: The NGT has benches in Delhi (principal), Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai (southern zone, covering AP).
events.today: It has fined states heavily for river pollution and waste.
events.mnemonic: Regulators by year "R-S-T-I-C-P": RBI 35, SEBI 92, TRAI 97, IRDAI 99, CCI 02, PFRDA 13.

events.title: First Administrative Reforms Commission
events.summary: The government sets up the First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) under Morarji Desai, later K. Hanumanthaiya. It gives 20 reports, including the idea of Lokpal and Lokayukta.
events.detail:
Second ARC (2005–09, Veerappa Moily, later V. Ramachandran) gave 15 reports: RTI, ethics in governance, citizen-centric administration, e-governance, local governance, public order and others.

Earlier reform reports: **A. D. Gorwala** (1951) and **Paul Appleby** (1953, 1956).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1966: four years after the Santhanam Committee.
events.before: The Santhanam Committee (1964) had shown deep corruption.
events.after: Maharashtra set up the first Lokayukta (1971); the Lokpal law came only in 2013.
events.today: The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances handles reform and CPGRAMS (online grievances).
events.mnemonic: ARCs "1-2 = 66-05": First (Morarji, 20 reports, Lokpal idea), Second (Moily, 15 reports).

events.title: Citizen's Charters begin in India
events.summary: A conference of Chief Ministers (May 1997) adopts an Action Plan for Effective and Responsive Government, including Citizen's Charters — public promises by each office on service standards and grievance redress.
events.detail:
The idea came from Britain (John Major, 1991). The **Sevottam** model (2006) set three parts: **citizen's charter**, **grievance redress**, **service delivery capability**. Some states passed **Right to Services** laws (Madhya Pradesh first, 2010).

**Social audit**: villagers check public works themselves — first used widely under MGNREGA in **Andhra Pradesh** (2006).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1997: 50 years of Independence.
events.before: Government offices made no promises on time or quality of service.
events.after: The Citizen's Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill (2011) lapsed; states took the lead with service laws.
events.today: AP's **Public Grievance Redressal System** (PGRS) and Telangana's Prajavani follow this idea.

events.title: Second Administrative Reforms Commission
events.summary: The Second ARC (August 2005) under Veerappa Moily studies how to make government proactive, accountable, transparent and citizen-friendly.
events.detail:
Good governance (World Bank, UNDP): **participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus, equity, effectiveness, accountability**. India marks **Good Governance Day** on 25 December (Vajpayee's birthday, since 2014).

ARC report 4 was "**Ethics in Governance**"; report 11 was "**Promoting e-Governance — the SMART Way**" (Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2005: the same year as the RTI Act.
events.before: The 1991 reforms changed the role of the state; the First ARC (1966) was 40 years old.
events.after: Many ideas were adopted (RTI training, e-governance, Lokpal).
events.today: AP's RTGS (2017) and "Mana Mitra" WhatsApp services (2025) apply the SMART idea.
events.mnemonic: SMART government = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent.

events.title: National e-Governance Plan (NeGP)
events.summary: The National e-Governance Plan (May 2006) launches 27 Mission Mode Projects (later 31) and common service centres to deliver government services online.
events.detail: Types of e-governance: **G2C** (government to citizen), **G2B** (business), **G2G**, **G2E** (employees). Early AP projects: **e-Seva** (2001, Hyderabad), **CARD** (property registration, 1998), **FRIENDS** (Kerala).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2006: one year after the 2nd ARC.
events.before: States like AP (e-Seva, CARD) and Karnataka (Bhoomi land records, 2000) had shown it could work.
events.after: **Digital India** (2015) built on NeGP; **e-Kranti** (NeGP 2.0, 2015).
events.today: Common Service Centres now number over 5 lakh.
events.mnemonic: e-governance "C-B-G-E": G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E.

events.title: First Aadhaar numbers issued
events.summary: On 29 September 2010 the first Aadhaar numbers are given at Tembhli village (Nandurbar, Maharashtra). The UIDAI (2009, Nandan Nilekani) issues a 12-digit number linked to fingerprints and iris.
events.detail: The **Aadhaar Act** (2016) gave it legal backing; **Puttaswamy (Aadhaar)** (2018) upheld it for welfare and tax but not for private bodies or school admissions. Aadhaar is the "A" in the **JAM trinity**.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 29 September 2010.
events.before: Many welfare cards were fake or duplicated.
events.after: Aadhaar-based DBT, e-KYC, and Aadhaar-enabled payments followed.
events.today: About 140 crore Aadhaar numbers have been issued.

events.title: Digital India launched
events.summary: Digital India is launched on 1 July 2015 with three aims: digital infrastructure for every citizen, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment.
