events.detail: Digital public infrastructure: **Aadhaar**, **UPI** (2016), **DigiLocker** (2015), **UMANG** (2017), **CoWIN** (2021), **ONDC** (2022), **BharatNet** (rural broadband), **GeM** (government shopping, 2016). AP: **RTGS** (2017) and **Mana Mitra** WhatsApp governance (2025).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1 July 2015: one year after the new government took office.
events.before: NeGP (2006) and Aadhaar (2010) had laid the base.
events.after: India's "India Stack" model was offered to other countries during its G20 presidency (2023).
events.today: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) governs data use.

events.title: AP Real Time Governance Society
events.summary: Andhra Pradesh sets up the Real Time Governance Society (2017) at Amaravati to watch welfare delivery, grievances and data from all departments on one dashboard.
events.detail: AP's governance tools: **RTGS**; the 1100 grievance number; **village and ward secretariats** (2019); **PGRS** (Public Grievance Redressal System); **Mana Mitra** WhatsApp governance (January 2025) offering hundreds of services by phone.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2017: two years after Digital India.
events.before: AP had pioneered e-Seva (2001) and CARD (1998).
events.after: The model was revived and expanded after 2024 with data lakes and AI.
events.today: AP calls its approach "data-driven governance".

events.title: National Integration Council set up
events.summary: After a National Integration Conference (September–October 1961), Nehru sets up the National Integration Council to fight communalism, casteism, regionalism and linguism.
events.detail:
Pressure groups: business (FICCI, CII), trade unions (AITUC, INTUC, BMS), farmers (Bharatiya Kisan Union), professional (IMA, Bar Council), and caste or religious groups. Unlike parties, they try to influence government without contesting elections.

Civil society and **NGOs**, **SHGs** (Self-Help Groups, linked to banks from 1992; DWCRA in AP from 1982) carry development to the grassroots.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1961: the year of the first census after reorganisation.
events.before: Language riots and the reorganisation of states (1956–60) raised fears for unity.
events.after: The council met irregularly (last major meeting 2013). The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions dealt with regional demands.
events.today: Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (31 October) promotes national unity.

events.title: FEMA replaces FERA
events.summary: The Foreign Exchange Management Act (1999, in force June 2000) replaces the strict Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (1973). Breaking foreign-exchange rules becomes a civil matter, not a crime.
events.detail: LPG milestones: new industrial policy (1991, licences ended for most industries), rupee devalued (1991), current-account convertibility (1994), **FEMA** (1999), **Competition Act** (2002, replaced MRTP 1969), **FRBM** (2003), **GST** (2017), **IBC** (2016).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1999: eight years after the 1991 reforms.
events.before: FERA (1973) made Coca-Cola and IBM leave India (1977) by forcing them to cut foreign shares.
events.after: Money-laundering was handled separately by the **PMLA** (2002).
events.today: The Enforcement Directorate enforces both FEMA and PMLA.
events.mnemonic: "FERA fears, FEMA manages": criminal (1973) → civil (1999).

events.title: Department of Disinvestment created
events.summary: The Vajpayee government creates a Department of Disinvestment (December 1999) to sell government shares in public-sector companies.
events.detail:
Steps: the **Rangarajan Committee** (1993) on disinvestment; strategic sales of **Modern Foods** (2000), **BALCO** (2001), **VSNL** and **Maruti** (2002–03). Later: **DIPAM** (2016), **Air India** sold to the Tata group (2022), **LIC IPO** (2022), and the **National Monetisation Pipeline** (2021).

FDI limits were raised step by step: 100% automatic in most sectors; 74% in defence (2020); the 2025 budget proposed raising insurance FDI to 100%.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: December 1999.
events.before: Many PSUs made losses; the 1991 reforms began selling small shares.
events.after: Privatisation slowed after 2004 and picked up again after 2014.
events.today: Visakhapatnam Steel's planned sale (2021) was later shelved with a revival package (2025).

events.title: BRICS New Development Bank agreed
events.summary: At the Fortaleza summit (July 2014) Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa agree to set up the New Development Bank (Shanghai) and a Contingent Reserve Arrangement. Its first president was India's K. V. Kamath.
events.detail: Development banks: **World Bank** group (1944), **ADB** (1966, Manila), **AIIB** (2016, Beijing; India is the second-largest shareholder), **NDB** (2015, Shanghai). Groupings: **SAARC** (1985), **BIMSTEC** (1997), **IBSA** (2003), **SCO** (India joined 2017), **Quad** (2017), **I2U2** (2022). Export-control regimes India joined: **MTCR** (2016), **Wassenaar** (2017), **Australia Group** (2018); not yet the **NSG**.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: July 2014; the bank opened in 2015.
events.before: Emerging economies felt the IMF and World Bank gave them too little say.
events.after: BRICS expanded (2024–25) with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE and Indonesia.
events.today: India chairs BRICS in 2026.
events.mnemonic: Export-control clubs "M-W-A, 16-17-18": MTCR, Wassenaar, Australia Group; NSG still blocked.

events.title: Gujral Doctrine for neighbours
events.summary: Foreign Minister (later PM) I. K. Gujral sets out five principles (1996): India gives to its smaller neighbours without asking for anything in return; no country lets its land be used against another; no interference; respect for sovereignty; disputes settled peacefully.
events.detail: Neighbourhood policies in order: **Panchsheel** (1954), **Gujral Doctrine** (1996), **Look East** (1991, Narasimha Rao) → **Act East** (2014), **Neighbourhood First** (2014), **SAGAR** (Security and Growth for All in the Region, 2015) → **MAHASAGAR** (2025).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1996: the Ganga waters treaty with Bangladesh followed the same year.
events.before: The end of the Cold War (1991) let India rethink its neighbourhood.
events.after: The **Ganga Water Treaty** with Bangladesh (December 1996) and better ties with Nepal followed.
events.today: "Neighbourhood First" is the current label.
events.mnemonic: Neighbourhood line "P-G-L-A-N-S": Panchsheel 54, Gujral 96, Look East 91, Act East 14, Neighbourhood First 14, SAGAR 15.

events.title: The Quad is revived
events.summary: India, the United States, Japan and Australia revive the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue at Manila (November 2017) to keep the Indo-Pacific "free and open". The first leaders' summit is held in 2021.
events.detail: Groupings India belongs to: **G20** (1999; summit level 2008), **BRICS** (2009), **SCO** (2017), **Quad** (2017), **I2U2** (2022), **IPEF** (2022). Corridors: **IMEC** (India-Middle East-Europe, G20 2023), **INSTC** (with Iran and Russia), **Chabahar** port (Iran).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: November 2017; first proposed 2007.
events.before: The Quad met once in 2007 and then lapsed after Chinese protests.
events.after: Malabar naval exercises include all four (since 2020).
events.today: Quad leaders last met in person at Wilmington, USA (September 2024).

events.title: India-US civil nuclear deal and NSG waiver
events.summary: After the NSG gives India a special waiver (6 September 2008), India and the US sign the "123 Agreement" (October 2008), ending 34 years of nuclear isolation since Pokhran-I.
events.detail: India's nuclear doctrine (2003): **credible minimum deterrence**, **No First Use**, massive retaliation, civilian control (Nuclear Command Authority). India has not signed the **NPT** (1968) or **CTBT** (1996). Treaties: **Panchsheel** (1954), **Indus** (1960), **Tashkent** (1966), **Indo-Soviet** (1971), **Simla** (1972), **Lahore** (1999).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 2008: ten years after Pokhran-II.
events.before: The Left withdrew support from the UPA over the deal; the government won a trust vote (July 2008).
events.after: Nuclear deals with France, Russia and others followed; the **Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act** (2010) slowed US projects.
events.today: The 2025 budget set up a Nuclear Energy Mission (100 GW by 2047) with private firms invited.
events.mnemonic: Nuclear line "B-74-98-03-08": Bhabha, Pokhran-I, Pokhran-II, doctrine, deal.

events.title: AP's "Super Six" promises
events.summary: The TDP-Jana Sena-BJP alliance wins the June 2024 Andhra Pradesh election on six flagship promises, the "Super Six", and starts carrying them out from late 2024.
events.detail:
The six (as promised): **jobs** for 20 lakh youth (and an allowance until then); **Talliki Vandanam** (money for each school child); **Annadata Sukhibhava** (yearly support to farmers, with PM-KISAN); **Aadabidda Nidhi** (monthly help to women); **Deepam** (three free gas cylinders a year); **free bus travel for women** (Stree Shakti).

They sit on central schemes through **DBT**: PM-KISAN, PM Ujjwala, Samagra Shiksha.
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: June 2024: Chandrababu Naidu sworn in on 12 June 2024.
events.before: The earlier government (2019-24) ran "Navaratnalu" welfare schemes with volunteers.
events.after: Deepam-2 began (November 2024); Talliki Vandanam and Annadata Sukhibhava were paid in 2025; free bus travel for women began on 15 August 2025.
events.today: Scheme amounts and dates are asked in Group-II; check the latest budget.
events.mnemonic: Super Six "J-T-A-A-D-B": Jobs, Talliki Vandanam, Annadata, Aadabidda, Deepam, Bus.

events.title: PM Surya Ghar: free electricity from rooftop solar
events.summary: Launched in February 2024, PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana aims to put rooftop solar panels on one crore homes with a subsidy, giving up to 300 units of free power a month.
events.detail: Other newer schemes: **PM Vishwakarma** (September 2023, for 18 traditional crafts), **PM-KUSUM** (2019, solar pumps for farmers), **PM Ujjwala** (2016, free LPG connections), **Lakhpati Didi** (2023, SHG women), **PM Internship Scheme** (2024).
events.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity and Governance in India; NCERT Class 12 Contemporary World Politics; 2nd ARC reports; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: February 2024: about a month after the Ram temple consecration (January 2024).
events.before: India set a target of 500 GW non-fossil power by 2030 (COP26, 2021).
events.after: Installations grew fast in 2024-25; Gujarat and Maharashtra lead.
events.today: It is one of the world's largest rooftop solar programmes.

events.title: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
events.summary: A new CrPC (1973, in force 1974) replaces the 1898 code and separates the judiciary from the executive: judicial magistrates try cases; executive magistrates (collectors, tahsildars) only keep the peace.
events.detail:
Criminal courts: **Supreme Court** → **High Court** → **Sessions Court** (can give the death sentence, confirmed by the High Court) → **Chief Judicial Magistrate** → **Judicial Magistrate** First and Second Class. Metropolitan magistrates in big cities.

Article 50 (DPSP) asks for separation of the judiciary from the executive — the 1973 code carried it out.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1973: the year of Kesavananda.
events.before: Under the 1898 code district magistrates both governed and judged.
events.after: The CrPC was replaced by the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** on 1 July 2024.
events.today: The BNSS keeps the court ladder but renames some magistrates.
events.mnemonic: Criminal court ladder "S-H-S-C-J": Supreme, High, Sessions, Chief Judicial, Judicial Magistrate.

events.title: Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 after the Nirbhaya case
events.summary: After the gang-rape and death of a young woman in Delhi (December 2012), the Justice J. S. Verma Committee reports in 29 days, and Parliament passes the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act (April 2013), widening the definition of rape and adding stalking, voyeurism and acid attack as crimes.
events.detail:
Basics: an **FIR** (Section 154 CrPC; now BNSS 173, including **Zero FIR** and **e-FIR**) is filed for **cognisable** offences — police can arrest without a warrant. **Bailable** offences give bail as a right; **non-bailable** ones at the court's discretion; **anticipatory bail** before arrest.

The **Nirbhaya Fund** (2013) pays for women's safety projects (one-stop centres, 181 helpline).
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: December 2012 → Verma report January 2013 → Act April 2013.
events.before: Women's groups had long demanded tougher rape laws (Mathura case, 1979, led to the 1983 amendment).
events.after: Four convicts were hanged in March 2020. The **Juvenile Justice Act** (2015) let 16–18-year-olds be tried as adults for heinous crimes.
events.today: The BNS (2024) keeps these offences in a separate chapter on crimes against women and children.

events.title: BNS, BNSS and BSA replace the colonial criminal laws
events.summary: On 1 July 2024 three new laws (passed December 2023) replace the Indian Penal Code (1860), the CrPC (1973) and the Indian Evidence Act (1872): the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.
events.detail: Key changes: **sedition** dropped, replaced by acts "endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity" (BNS 152); **mob lynching** and **organised crime** become offences; **community service** as a punishment; **Zero FIR** and e-FIR; forensic teams for crimes with 7+ years' punishment; trials in absentia; electronic evidence on par with documents.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1 July 2024: 164 years after the IPC (1860).
events.before: The IPC came from Macaulay's Law Commission (1837) and the 1860 Act.
events.after: Courts and police trained on the new sections; pending cases continue under the old laws.
events.today: BNS has 358 sections (IPC had 511).
events.mnemonic: Old → new "IPC → BNS, CrPC → BNSS, IEA → BSA" (punish, procedure, proof).

events.title: Four labour codes come into force
events.summary: On 21 November 2025 the four labour codes passed in 2019–20 come into force, replacing 29 central labour laws: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code.
events.detail:
Labour is in the **Concurrent List**. Earlier laws: **Factories Act** (1948), **Minimum Wages Act** (1948), **Industrial Disputes Act** (1947), **ESI** (1948), **EPF** (1952). Commissions: **Royal Commission on Labour** (Whitley, 1929), **First National Commission on Labour** (Gajendragadkar, 1969), **Second** (Ravindra Varma, 2002, suggested the codes).

Other welfare laws: **Consumer Protection Act** (2019), **IT Act** (2000) on cyber crime.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 21 November 2025: five years after the last codes were passed (2020).
events.before: Workers and employers had to follow dozens of overlapping laws.
events.after: The codes cover gig and platform workers under social security for the first time.
events.today: States are framing rules under the codes.
events.mnemonic: Four codes "W-I-S-O": Wages, Industrial relations, Social security, OSH.

events.title: Indian Institute of Public Administration founded
events.summary: On Paul Appleby's advice, the Indian Institute of Public Administration is set up in New Delhi (1954) with Nehru as its first president, to study and teach public administration.
events.detail:
Indian thinkers: **Kautilya** (Arthashastra), Gandhi (decentralisation, trusteeship). Western thinkers: **Weber** (bureaucracy), **Taylor** (scientific management), **Fayol** (14 principles), **Mayo** (Hawthorne, human relations), **Simon** (decision-making), **Maslow** (needs), **McGregor** (Theory X and Y), **Riggs** (ecological approach, "prismatic society").

Indian evolution: Kautilya → Mughal mansabdari → British ICS and districts → IAS and planning → Panchayati Raj → e-governance.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1954: one year after Appleby's first report (1953).
events.before: **A. D. Gorwala** (1951) and **Paul Appleby** (1953) reported on Indian administration after Independence.
events.after: The **Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration** (Mussoorie, 1959) trains IAS officers.
events.today: IIPA publishes the Indian Journal of Public Administration.
events.mnemonic: Motivation thinkers "M-M-H": Maslow (needs ladder), McGregor (X and Y), Herzberg (two factors).

events.title: All India Services Act, 1951
events.summary: Parliament passes the All India Services Act (1951) under Article 312, giving legal form to the IAS and IPS, which Patel had created in 1946–47 to replace the ICS and IP. The Indian Forest Service follows in 1966.
events.detail:
All-India service officers are recruited by the **Centre (UPSC)** but serve in **state cadres**; only the Centre can dismiss them. The Rajya Sabha can create a new all-India service by a two-thirds resolution (Article 312).

AP structure: the **Chief Secretary** heads the secretariat; **District Collector** runs each district; **RDO** (revenue division), **tahsildar** (mandal), **VRO** and village secretariats below. Reforms: **Hota Committee** (2004), **2nd ARC** (2005–09), **Mission Karmayogi** (2020, training).
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1951: the same year as the First Amendment.
events.before: The ICS ("steel frame") was the British backbone; Patel defended keeping an all-India service at the Premiers' Conference (1946).
events.after: Civil Services Day (21 April) marks Patel's 1947 speech to the first IAS probationers.
events.today: Mission Karmayogi (2020) trains officers through the iGOT platform.
events.mnemonic: All-India services "IAS-IPS-IFoS": two in 1951 (from ICS and IP), forest in 1966.

events.title: Asch's conformity experiment
events.summary: Solomon Asch (USA) shows that many people give an obviously wrong answer about the length of lines just because the rest of the group does (1951) — the pull of conformity.
events.detail: Classic social-influence studies: **Sherif** (autokinetic effect, norms, 1935), **Asch** (conformity, 1951), **Festinger** (cognitive dissonance, 1957), **Milgram** (obedience, 1961–63), **Zimbardo** (Stanford prison, 1971). Attitude scales: **Thurstone** (1928), **Likert** (1932), **Bogardus** social distance (1925), **semantic differential** (Osgood, 1957).
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1951: the year of India's first general elections.
events.before: Sherif (1935) had shown how group norms form.
events.after: Group pressure and conformity are used to explain "groupthink" in bureaucracies (Janis, 1972).
events.today: Exams ask for the experiment behind each idea.

events.title: Katz's functional theory of attitudes
events.summary: Daniel Katz (1960) explains that attitudes serve four needs: utilitarian (to gain rewards), knowledge (to make sense of the world), ego-defensive (to protect self-image) and value-expressive (to show who we are).
events.detail: An attitude is a learned, lasting way of feeling and acting towards a person, object or idea. Its parts (**ABC model**): **Affective** (feeling), **Behavioural** (action), **Cognitive** (belief). Attitudes can be **explicit** or **implicit**, strong or weak.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1960: three years after Festinger's dissonance theory (1957).
events.before: Allport (1935) called attitude the most important idea in social psychology.
events.after: Persuasion research (Hovland's Yale school, the Elaboration Likelihood Model of Petty and Cacioppo, 1980s) built on it.
events.today: Used to design behaviour-change campaigns like Swachh Bharat.
events.mnemonic: Attitude ABC = Affect, Behaviour, Cognition; Katz's four functions "U-K-E-V".

events.title: Festinger's cognitive dissonance
events.summary: Leon Festinger (1957) shows that when our actions and beliefs clash, we feel discomfort (dissonance) and often change the belief to match the action.
events.detail: Attitude formation: **classical conditioning**, **operant conditioning** (rewards and punishments), **observational learning** (Bandura, 1961–63), direct experience, family and peers. Attitude change: persuasion (source, message, audience), dissonance, and new experience. Attitude and behaviour are linked weakly unless the attitude is strong and specific (Ajzen's **theory of planned behaviour**, 1991).
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1957: the year of India's second general elections.
events.before: Behaviourists (Skinner) had explained behaviour by rewards alone.
events.after: Dissonance helps explain why officials justify rule-breaking once they start.
events.today: Nudge theory (Thaler, Nobel 2017) uses such ideas in public policy.

events.title: Kohlberg's stages of moral development
events.summary: Lawrence Kohlberg (1958) describes six stages of moral reasoning in three levels: pre-conventional (avoid punishment, seek reward), conventional (good boy/girl, law and order) and post-conventional (social contract, universal principles).
events.detail: **Moral attitudes** are beliefs about right and wrong (honesty, fairness); **political attitudes** are views on power and policy (liberal, conservative, radical, reactionary). Both shape how a civil servant acts. **Carol Gilligan** (1982) added an "ethics of care".
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1958: built on Jean Piaget's work.
events.before: Piaget (1932) studied how children judge right and wrong.
events.after: Used in ethics training: a good officer should act at the post-conventional level.
events.today: A standard ethics-paper concept.
events.mnemonic: Kohlberg "3 levels × 2 = 6 stages": Pre-conventional, Conventional, Post-conventional.

events.title: Milgram's obedience experiment
events.summary: Stanley Milgram (Yale, 1961) finds that about two-thirds of ordinary people will give what they think are dangerous electric shocks to another person when an authority figure tells them to.
events.detail: Social influence: **conformity** (going along with the group), **compliance** (agreeing to a request), **obedience** (following authority). Persuasion techniques: foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-ball. Sources of credibility: expertise and trustworthiness.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1961: the year of Adolf Eichmann's trial, which inspired it.
events.before: After the Holocaust people asked how ordinary officials obeyed evil orders (Hannah Arendt's "banality of evil").
events.after: It shaped rules on research ethics and the debate on "just following orders" in bureaucracy.
events.today: Used to teach why officials must refuse illegal orders.

events.title: Goleman popularises emotional intelligence
events.summary: Daniel Goleman's book Emotional Intelligence (1995) argues that knowing and managing feelings matters as much as IQ. He names five parts: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.
events.detail:
Models: **Salovey and Mayer** (1990, the ability model — perceive, use, understand, manage emotions), **Goleman** (mixed model), **Bar-On** (EQ-i). In governance EI helps in crisis management, team leadership and dealing with angry citizens.

Foundational values for civil service (2nd ARC): integrity, impartiality and non-partisanship, objectivity, dedication, empathy, tolerance and compassion towards weaker sections.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1995: the same year as the Nolan Committee in Britain.
events.before: Howard Gardner (1983) proposed multiple intelligences, including interpersonal and intrapersonal.
events.after: EI training became part of civil-service and police training (Mission Karmayogi).
events.today: A favourite case-study theme in the ethics paper.
events.mnemonic: Goleman's five "S-S-M-E-S": Self-awareness, Self-regulation, Motivation, Empathy, Social skills.

events.title: Cadbury Report on corporate governance
events.summary: Britain's Cadbury Committee (1992) sets the first modern code of corporate governance: independent directors, separate chairman and CEO, audit committees and honest reporting.
events.detail:
In India: the **Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee** (1999) → SEBI's **Clause 49**; the **Satyam** scam (2009, Hyderabad) → the **Companies Act, 2013** (independent directors, **CSR** — 2% of profit for companies above a size; India was the first country to make CSR mandatory).

Ethics in international relations: just war, humanitarian aid, refugees, climate justice ("common but differentiated responsibilities"). Funding ethics: tied aid, NGO funding (**FCRA**, 2010).
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1992: one year after India's 1991 reforms.
events.before: Company scandals in Britain (Maxwell, BCCI) shocked investors.
events.after: The US Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) followed Enron; India's Companies Act (2013) followed Satyam.
events.today: SEBI's LODR rules (2015) replaced Clause 49.

events.title: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
events.summary: Parliament passes the Prevention of Corruption Act (1988), which defines a "public servant" widely and punishes taking bribes and having assets beyond known income. The 2018 amendment also punishes giving a bribe.
events.detail:
Anti-corruption architecture: **PCA** (1988), **CVC** (1964/2003), **CBI** (1963), **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act** (2013), **Whistle Blowers Protection Act** (2014), **Benami Transactions** law (1988, strengthened 2016), **PMLA** (2002), **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act** (2018). India ratified the **UN Convention against Corruption** (UNCAC) in 2011.

Section 17A (2018) needs prior government approval before probing an officer's decisions.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1988: the year the Bofors scandal broke into the open (1987–89).
events.before: The 1947 Prevention of Corruption Act was too narrow.
events.after: The 2018 amendment made bribe-giving a crime and protected honest decisions.
events.today: Transparency International ranks India in its Corruption Perceptions Index every year.

events.title: Nolan Committee: seven principles of public life
events.summary: Britain's Committee on Standards in Public Life under Lord Nolan (1995) sets seven principles for anyone holding public office: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership.
events.detail:
**Probity** means strict honesty and uprightness in public life — more than following rules. The 2nd ARC's **Ethics in Governance** report (2007) drew on Nolan and suggested a code of ethics for ministers and civil servants and a **Public Services Bill**.

Values in public administration: integrity, impartiality, neutrality, accountability, transparency, empathy, dedication to public service.
events.source: Lexicon / Subba Rao & Roy Chowdhury, Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude; 2nd ARC reports; Laxmikanth, Public Administration; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1995: the same year as Goleman's Emotional Intelligence.
events.before: "Cash for questions" scandals in the British Parliament (1994).
events.after: Many countries, and India's 2nd ARC (2007), used the principles.
events.today: The All India Services (Conduct) Rules (1968) are India's formal code for officers.
events.mnemonic: Nolan seven "S-I-O-A-O-H-L" ("Some Indians Only Act On High Laws"): Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty, Leadership.
